proposition_tested: P1.1 Retained review driven by formal obligations irrespective of transparency
observed_finding: PCAOB amendments make the auditor's work effort to evaluate a specialist's work risk-based and scalable: commensurate with the risk of material misstatement (RMM) and the significance of the specialist's work. For a company's specialist, four factors set required persuasiveness: significance of the work, RMM, the company's ability to affect the specialist's judgments, and the specialist's knowledge, skill and ability. Effort is greatest when RMM is high, work is critical, competence is lower and company influence is high.
population_and_setting: US public-company audits under PCAOB standards; FY ending on/after 2020-12-15
study_or_observation_method: Regulatory text / rule filing description
outcome_measured: Required extent of auditor evaluation of specialists' work
quantitative_result: null (qualitative scaling factors)
source_locator: 84 FR 13442 (Summary); 84 FR 13458-13459 (four factors, Figure 4)
short_exact_excerpt: the auditor should obtain more persuasive evidence as the significance of the specialist's work, the risk of material misstatement, or the ability of the company to affect the specialist's judgments increases
limitations: Obligation, not observed effort. The listed scaling factors do not include the transparency or documentation quality of the specialist's report; transparency enters only indirectly via what procedures are feasible.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a regulated receiver (auditor) must evaluate outside analysis it uses; analog to IC/credit team relying on advisor/consultant reports (e.g., independent engineer, energy yield, model audit). Similarity: producer->accountable receiver->opinion/decision. Differences: audit duties are legally mandated and inspected; investment committees' review duties come from internal policy, fiduciary duty and lender requirements, so the mandated floor may be lower or differently shaped. Needs verification: whether IC/credit policies impose comparable non-delegable evaluation duties.
analyst_inference: The mandated floor (W1) scales with stakes, competence and objectivity of the producer, not with how well the producer documents. Better documentation can change HOW the receiver satisfies the duty (see WS1-E03) but not WHETHER it must be satisfied.

proposition_tested: P1.1 obligations; P2.1 provenance relevant to verification
observed_finding: New AS 1105 Appendix A requires the auditor, when using a company specialist's work as evidence, to understand the specialist's work and report(s) and related company processes/controls, assess knowledge, skill, ability and relationship to the company, and evaluate (i) the data, significant assumptions and methods (including models) used, and (ii) the relevance and reliability of the work and its relationship to the assertion. AS 1210 (auditor-engaged) and AS 1201 App. C (auditor-employed) require evaluating whether findings and conclusions are consistent with the work performed.
population_and_setting: US PCAOB audits
study_or_observation_method: Regulatory text / rule filing description
outcome_measured: Elements the receiver must evaluate
quantitative_result: null
source_locator: 84 FR 13442-13443 (bulleted summary of Appendix A, Appendix C, AS 1210)
short_exact_excerpt: Performing procedures to evaluate the work of a company's specialist, including evaluating: (i) The data, significant assumptions, and methods (which may include models) used by the specialist
limitations: Describes required evaluation objects, not how much time each takes.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a regulated receiver (auditor) must evaluate outside analysis it uses; analog to IC/credit team relying on advisor/consultant reports (e.g., independent engineer, energy yield, model audit). Similarity: producer->accountable receiver->opinion/decision. Differences: audit duties are legally mandated and inspected; investment committees' review duties come from internal policy, fiduciary duty and lender requirements, so the mandated floor may be lower or differently shaped. Needs verification: whether IC/credit policies impose comparable non-delegable evaluation duties. The objects named (data, assumptions, methods, consistency of conclusions with work performed) map directly onto what an evidence-traceable advisor product would expose.
analyst_inference: The checklist of evaluation objects is exactly the information an inspectable advisor output would need to surface; the standard thus defines the receiver's demand for X3 (data provenance) and method/assumption disclosure.

proposition_tested: P2.1 Access to documentation/provenance reduces verification effort; P1.2 avoidable reconstruction
observed_finding: The amendments do not require access to a specialist's proprietary model; the auditor must obtain information to assess whether the model conforms to the reporting framework. Depending on factors, this may involve understanding the model, reviewing descriptions of the model in the specialist's report, testing controls over the company's evaluation of the specialist, or assessing inputs and outputs (if necessary using an alternative model). For auditor-engaged specialists, the necessary access to a model depends on significance, RMM, and the specialist's competence.
population_and_setting: US PCAOB audits; specialists with proprietary models (e.g., pricing/valuation)
study_or_observation_method: Regulatory text and Board response to commenters
intervention_and_comparator: Documentation-based route (model description in report) vs alternative-model / input-output testing route
outcome_measured: Permissible means of satisfying evaluation duty
quantitative_result: null
source_locator: 84 FR 13457-13458 (company's specialist models); 84 FR 13467 (auditor-engaged, AS 1210.10); excerpt spans the page break between 84 FR 13457 and 13458
short_exact_excerpt: reviewing descriptions of the model in the specialist's report or equivalent communication, testing controls over the company's evaluation of the specialist's work, or assessing the inputs to and output from the model (if necessary, using an alternative model for comparison)
limitations: Lists alternatives without ranking their cost; does not show that documentation route is cheaper in practice.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a regulated receiver (auditor) must evaluate outside analysis it uses; analog to IC/credit team relying on advisor/consultant reports (e.g., independent engineer, energy yield, model audit). Similarity: producer->accountable receiver->opinion/decision. Differences: audit duties are legally mandated and inspected; investment committees' review duties come from internal policy, fiduciary duty and lender requirements, so the mandated floor may be lower or differently shaped. Needs verification: whether IC/credit policies impose comparable non-delegable evaluation duties. Direct analog: advisor's proprietary models/tools; a clear model description may substitute for rebuilding.
analyst_inference: Standard-level recognition that producer documentation of method can substitute for receiver reconstruction (alternative model) — the closest public-standard analog to P1.2/P2.1. When descriptions are absent, the fallback is building an alternative model: W2 reconstruction caused by opacity.

proposition_tested: P2.4 Visibility into scope, limitations and omissions affects appropriate reliance
observed_finding: AS 1105.A10 requires additional procedures as necessary if the specialist's findings appear to contradict the assertion or the work does not provide sufficient evidence; additional procedures are ordinarily necessary when the specialist's report contains restrictions, disclaimers or limitations regarding the auditor's use, or a conflict of interest is identified. Example: a report stating values are not an indication of fair value generally would not provide sufficient evidence for fair value.
population_and_setting: US PCAOB audits
study_or_observation_method: Regulatory text
outcome_measured: Trigger for additional receiver procedures
quantitative_result: null
source_locator: 84 FR 13460 (AS 1105.A9-.A10 discussion, incl. fn 89)
short_exact_excerpt: A specialist's report may contain restrictions, disclaimers, or limitations that cast doubt on the relevance and reliability of the information contained in the specialist's report
limitations: Obligation; frequency in practice unknown.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a regulated receiver (auditor) must evaluate outside analysis it uses; analog to IC/credit team relying on advisor/consultant reports (e.g., independent engineer, energy yield, model audit). Similarity: producer->accountable receiver->opinion/decision. Differences: audit duties are legally mandated and inspected; investment committees' review duties come from internal policy, fiduciary duty and lender requirements, so the mandated floor may be lower or differently shaped. Needs verification: whether IC/credit policies impose comparable non-delegable evaluation duties. Advisor reports with heavy disclaimers/reliance limitations would, by analogy, push extra work back to the IC/lender.
analyst_inference: Explicit scope/limitation statements are treated as decision-relevant information that redirects receiver work; producer boilerplate limitations are not costless to the receiver.

proposition_tested: P1.6 Review persists beyond rational need (tested inversely: is under-review the observed failure?)
observed_finding: PCAOB inspection observations (pre-2020) included auditors using a company specialist's work without: evaluating reasonableness of assumptions; understanding methods or assumptions; testing accuracy/completeness of company data used by the specialist; or evaluating qualifications. For auditors' own specialists (more common findings), auditors did not reach an understanding of responsibilities, adequately evaluate the specialist's work, or consider contradictory evidence/resolve discrepancies the specialist identified. SEC/PCAOB enforcement cases alleged similar failures.
population_and_setting: PCAOB-inspected US audits, several years before 2018
study_or_observation_method: Regulator summary of inspection findings and enforcement
outcome_measured: Types of deficiency
quantitative_result: not reported (no counts given)
source_locator: 84 FR 13447-13448 ('Observations From Audit Inspections and Enforcement Cases')
short_exact_excerpt: consider contradictory evidence identified by the specialist or resolve discrepancies or other concerns that the specialist identified
limitations: No frequencies; risk-based inspection selection; describes failures, not average practice.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a regulated receiver (auditor) must evaluate outside analysis it uses; analog to IC/credit team relying on advisor/consultant reports (e.g., independent engineer, energy yield, model audit). Similarity: producer->accountable receiver->opinion/decision. Differences: audit duties are legally mandated and inspected; investment committees' review duties come from internal policy, fiduciary duty and lender requirements, so the mandated floor may be lower or differently shaped. Needs verification: whether IC/credit policies impose comparable non-delegable evaluation duties.
analyst_inference: The regulator's documented failure mode is too LITTLE receiver evaluation (over-reliance), including ignoring problems the producer itself flagged. This challenges a framing in which receiver review is mainly excess ritual, and shows that surfacing an issue in the producer's output does not guarantee the receiver acts on it.

proposition_tested: P-NEW: Earlier and more frequent producer-receiver coordination reduces evaluation deficiencies
observed_finding: Some firms remediated specialist-related findings mostly by enhancing methodologies to improve coordination between auditor and auditor's specialist through earlier and more frequent communications; the PCAOB says these may have contributed, at least in part, to a decline in findings for auditor's specialists. No similar change was seen in findings on company specialists (whom the auditor does not direct).
population_and_setting: PCAOB-inspected firms, pre-2018
study_or_observation_method: Regulator observation of remedial actions and finding trends
outcome_measured: Frequency of inspection findings
quantitative_result: not reported
short_exact_excerpt: In most cases, such actions included enhancements to firm methodologies to improve coordination between the auditor and the auditor's specialist through earlier and more frequent communications.
limitations: Correlational; 'may have contributed, at least in part'; no counts.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a regulated receiver (auditor) must evaluate outside analysis it uses; analog to IC/credit team relying on advisor/consultant reports (e.g., independent engineer, energy yield, model audit). Similarity: producer->accountable receiver->opinion/decision. Differences: audit duties are legally mandated and inspected; investment committees' review duties come from internal policy, fiduciary duty and lender requirements, so the mandated floor may be lower or differently shaped. Needs verification: whether IC/credit policies impose comparable non-delegable evaluation duties. Suggests scoping/integration upstream (agreeing what the advisor will check and deliver) may matter as much as output format.
analyst_inference: Process integration (early agreement on scope and communication), rather than output transparency alone, is the regulator's reported lever for fewer receiver failures; relevant to RQ3 but not a test of output-level traceability.

proposition_tested: P1.2 Opacity causes avoidable reconstruction (qualified: opacity may instead cause shallower review)
observed_finding: PCAOB economic analysis: specialists' work is highly technical and often not entirely transparent to the auditor, who may lack complete access or comparable expertise; because evaluating/supervising specialists is relatively costly, auditors may have incentives to forgo procedures. Evaluating a company's specialist (no contractual relationship, proprietary data, less familiarity) requires greater effort than evaluating the auditor's own specialist.
population_and_setting: US PCAOB audits
study_or_observation_method: Regulator economic reasoning citing literature and comments
outcome_measured: Cost and incentives of evaluating specialists
quantitative_result: null
short_exact_excerpt: the specialist's work is highly technical in nature and often is not entirely transparent to the auditor, who may not have complete access to the specialist's work
limitations: Theoretical/economic reasoning, not measurement.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a regulated receiver (auditor) must evaluate outside analysis it uses; analog to IC/credit team relying on advisor/consultant reports (e.g., independent engineer, energy yield, model audit). Similarity: producer->accountable receiver->opinion/decision. Differences: audit duties are legally mandated and inspected; investment committees' review duties come from internal policy, fiduciary duty and lender requirements, so the mandated floor may be lower or differently shaped. Needs verification: whether IC/credit policies impose comparable non-delegable evaluation duties.
analyst_inference: Opacity raises evaluation cost, but the regulator predicts the response is under-performance of procedures, not necessarily reconstruction. So opacity may show up as risk (W1 shortfall) rather than as visible extra work (W2) — important for measuring 'avoidable reconstruction'.

proposition_tested: P1.1 Obligations drive retained work (magnitude of incremental mandated effort)
observed_finding: After the strengthened estimates/specialists requirements took effect, about one-third of surveyed firms reported improved practices; others reported limited effects because methodologies were already aligned. The majority of interviewed engagement partners estimated additional time at less than 1% of total audit hours; none reported raising fees. Most commonly reported specialist-related effects: improved coordination/communication with auditors' specialists and enhanced documentation of the work performed by specialists.
population_and_setting: 17 US audit firms (9 annually inspected, 8 triennially inspected); 31 engagement partners; 12 audit committee chairs and 9 preparers; 14 comment letters
study_or_observation_method: Survey, interviews, comment letters (targeted non-random sample)
intervention_and_comparator: Pre vs post implementation of new requirements (FY ending on/after 2020-12-15)
outcome_measured: Self-reported audit hours, fees, practice changes
quantitative_result: Majority of 31 partners: additional time <1% of total audit hours; 0 partners reported fee increases; ~1/3 of 17 firms reported improved practices
source_locator: PCAOB Release 2022-008, pp. 3-4 (Key Findings), p. 6 (Engagement Partner Interviews) (two-column PDF layout; excerpt read across column line breaks)
short_exact_excerpt: The majority of engagement partners interviewed estimated that the additional time spent was less than 1% of total audit hours.
limitations: Self-reported; targeted 'upper bound' sample; regulator evaluating own rule; estimates and specialists rules not separable.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a regulated receiver (auditor) must evaluate outside analysis it uses; analog to IC/credit team relying on advisor/consultant reports (e.g., independent engineer, energy yield, model audit). Similarity: producer->accountable receiver->opinion/decision. Differences: audit duties are legally mandated and inspected; investment committees' review duties come from internal policy, fiduciary duty and lender requirements, so the mandated floor may be lower or differently shaped. Needs verification: whether IC/credit policies impose comparable non-delegable evaluation duties.
analyst_inference: Tightening the mandated floor produced small measured effort changes, mainly documentation and coordination. This suggests W1 effort in audit is largely institutionalized already; it does not tell us how much of existing effort is W2.

proposition_tested: P-NEW: Receiver documentation demands induce producers to supply richer supporting evidence (producer-side response)
observed_finding: In the public comment input, some commenters reported increased auditor effort to understand and document assumptions underlying estimates, and a valuation service provider stated that its staff provided more robust pricing information to address auditors' demands for more extensive documentation.

outcome_measured: Reported changes in practice
quantitative_result: null (single commenter)
source_locator: PCAOB Release 2022-008, p. 8 (Public Request for Comment) (two-column PDF layout; excerpt read across column line breaks)

limitations: Single anecdotal commenter; no data on cost, pricing, or effect on auditor effort.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a regulated receiver (auditor) must evaluate outside analysis it uses; analog to IC/credit team relying on advisor/consultant reports (e.g., independent engineer, energy yield, model audit). Differences: audit duties are legally mandated and inspected; investment committees' review duties come from internal policy, fiduciary duty and lender requirements, so the mandated floor may be lower or differently shaped. proposition_tested: P3.2 Integration/new requirements shift effort rather than remove it
observed_finding: Large-sample analysis of inspections data (descriptive, not causal): probability an engagement used one or more auditor-employed specialists rose by a statistically significant 4.8 percentage points post-implementation, and probability of using company specialists' work rose 10.5 pp, both driven by smaller firms. Among engagements using auditor-employed specialists, hours per engagement did not change significantly, but the share of their hours in the preliminary (planning) phase rose 2.3 pp.
population_and_setting: PCAOB inspections data, pre vs post FY2020
study_or_observation_method: Descriptive pre/post comparison; no control group
intervention_and_comparator: Post- vs pre-implementation
outcome_measured: Specialist usage, specialist hours, phase allocation
quantitative_result: +4.8 pp (auditor-employed specialist use); +10.5 pp (company specialist use); no significant change in specialist hours per engagement; +2.3 pp share of specialist hours in preliminary phase
source_locator: PCAOB Release 2022-008, pp. 7-8 (Large-Sample Statistical Analysis; fn 12) (two-column PDF layout; excerpt read across column line breaks)
short_exact_excerpt: the proportion of auditor-employed specialist hours allocated to the preliminary phase of the audit increased by 2.3 percentage points
limitations: Confounded by COVID and other rule changes (staff explicitly say not causal).
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a regulated receiver (auditor) must evaluate outside analysis it uses; analog to IC/credit team relying on advisor/consultant reports (e.g., independent engineer, energy yield, model audit). Differences: audit duties are legally mandated and inspected; investment committees' review duties come from internal policy, fiduciary duty and lender requirements, so the mandated floor may be lower or differently shaped. Needs verification: whether IC/credit policies impose comparable non-delegable evaluation duties.
analyst_inference: Requirements moved specialist effort earlier (planning/scoping) without raising total specialist hours — consistent with effort being re-sequenced rather than eliminated.

proposition_tested: P1.1 Non-delegable responsibility persists irrespective of producer transparency
observed_finding: ISA 620: the auditor has sole responsibility for the audit opinion, not reduced by using an auditor's expert; the auditor shall not refer to the expert's work in an unmodified report unless law requires, and if required must state the reference does not reduce the auditor's responsibility.

study_or_observation_method: Standard text
outcome_measured: Allocation of responsibility
quantitative_result: null

proposition_tested: P2.4 Receiver work scales with producer track record and quality control (P-NEW: familiarity reduces required work)
observed_finding: ISA 620 para 8: nature, timing and extent of procedures vary with circumstances, considering (a) nature of the matter, (b) RMM, (c) significance of the expert's work, (d) the auditor's knowledge of and experience with previous work performed by that expert, and (e) whether the expert is subject to the auditor's firm's quality control policies and procedures.
population_and_setting: Audits under ISAs
study_or_observation_method: Standard text
outcome_measured: Determinants of extent of receiver procedures
quantitative_result: null
source_locator: ISA (UK) 620 para 8 (PDF p. 6)
short_exact_excerpt: The auditor's knowledge of and experience with previous work performed by that expert
limitations: Factors are to be 'considered'; no weights.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a regulated receiver (auditor) must evaluate outside analysis it uses; analog to IC/credit team relying on advisor/consultant reports (e.g., independent engineer, energy yield, model audit). proposition_tested: P2.1/P2.4 Producer disclosure of scope, standards, errors encountered and tests performed reduces/redirects receiver work
observed_finding: ISA 620 para 12 requires evaluating relevance/reasonableness of findings and consistency with other evidence, assumptions and methods, and relevance/completeness/accuracy of significant source data. A33 lists procedures: inquiries, reviewing the expert's working papers and reports, corroborative procedures (incl. reperforming calculations). A34 relevant factors include whether findings are clearly expressed with reference to agreed objectives, scope of work performed and standards applied; subject to reservations/limitations; based on appropriate consideration of errors or deviations encountered. A39: where the expert has tested source data, inquiry of the expert or supervision/review of the expert's tests may be an appropriate way to evaluate the data.

study_or_observation_method: Standard text
outcome_measured: Means of evaluating expert work
quantitative_result: null
source_locator: ISA (UK) 620 para 12; A33-A34 (PDF p. 16); A38-A39 (PDF p. 17)
short_exact_excerpt: If the auditor's expert has tested the source data, inquiry of that expert by the auditor, or supervision or review of that expert's tests may be an appropriate way for the auditor to evaluate that data's relevance, completeness, and accuracy.
limitations: Guidance ('may'); does not quantify savings.

Some respondents (incl. the Monitoring Group member) sought more explicit requirements, and some wanted written information from external experts on objectivity.

observed_finding: Survey of 32 audit partners/senior managers (5 firms). proposition_tested: P2.1 (challenged) More specific producer explanation increases elaboration/time; P2.3/P2.4 specificity changes reliance pattern
observed_finding: 2x2 between-subjects experiment with 98 audit managers (avg 6.94 years experience): source of specialist evidence (human firm specialist vs firm's proprietary AI system) x specificity of the specialist memo's discussion of methodology and assumptions (brief outline vs more thorough discussion with an added section on specific factors). With a less specific memo, auditors relied less on the system than the human (algorithm aversion); with a more specific memo the source difference disappeared, reliance on the human specialist directionally fell and on the system rose. Participants given the more specific memo took longer (marginal). Assumptions were rated more subjective when a human (vs system) gave the more specific explanation.

study_or_observation_method: Randomized 2x2 experiment
intervention_and_comparator: Human vs AI-system specialist; less vs more specific methodology/assumption explanation

proposition_tested: P2.5 Citations/traceability do not guarantee correctness or completeness.

Text reports Westlaw accuracy as 41% and Practical Law as 19% (revalidation moved it to 20%, fn 18). 95% CIs shown graphically only; n=202 queries.

In energy diligence, a cited permit, PPA clause or resource report may exist yet not say what the summary claims. Need to verify: error rates of source-linked diligence summaries on project documents (contracts, IE reports), which are more closed-universe than open legal research.
analyst_inference: Citations make verification possible but not unnecessary; the residual error rate (not the presence of citations) determines how much checking a rational recipient must keep.

proposition_tested: P2.1 Access to sources/provenance reduces verification time/effort (qualified); P2.3 citations can increase apparent reliability without correctness.
observed_finding: The authors classify 'misgrounded' answers (real source cited for a proposition it does not support) as hallucinations and state these are more dangerous than outright fabrication because they are subtler; detecting them requires opening cited sources, reading them, assessing authority and comparing them to the claim. One example cited a real, positively-flagged case whose description of an overruled case produced an incorrect answer.
evidence_type: analytic argument with illustrative examples within an empirical study
population_and_setting: Commercial legal RAG tools, 2024.
study_or_observation_method: Coding framework definition and qualitative error examples.
outcome_measured: Nature of errors and what checking them requires (not timed).
source_locator: arXiv v1, Section 4.3 (Hallucination), p. 9, incl. fn 10-11
short_exact_excerpt: Checking for these kinds of hallucinations requires users to click through to cited references, read and understand the relevant sources, assess their authority, and compare them to the propositions the model seeks to support.
limitations: No measurement of verification time or detection rates by users; the claim that misgrounding is harder to spot is argued, not tested.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Direct analog for source-linked diligence memos: a link to the right document does not remove the need to read the cited passage when the claim is consequential. Verify whether pinpoint (page/clause-level) links plus quoted text materially shorten this check compared with document-level links.
analyst_inference: Traceability lowers the cost of locating evidence (search cost) but not the cost of judging whether evidence supports the claim (comprehension cost); a product that only adds links may shift rather than remove review work.

proposition_tested: P2.4 Visibility into scope, checks performed, omissions, and uncertainty improves appropriate reliance (absence case).
observed_finding: The authors argue that because vendors provide no specific information on where their tools are reliable or where caution is needed, and because performance differs across tools and may change over time, lawyers must either verify by hand every proposition and citation (eroding efficiency gains) or rely without the information their competence and supervision duties require. Footnote 11 quotes a law-firm assessment that the need to verify output makes efficiency gains difficult to measure.
evidence_type: analytic argument (authors' interpretation of their results and professional rules)
population_and_setting: U.S. lawyers using commercial legal AI; professional responsibility rules.
study_or_observation_method: Discussion section reasoning.
source_locator: arXiv v1, Section 8.1, p. 23; fn 11, p. 9 (quoting Gottlieb 2024)
short_exact_excerpt: either verify by hand each and every proposition and citation produced by these tools (thereby undercutting the efficiency gains that AI is promised to provide)
limitations: Argument, not observed behavior; does not show that disclosure of reliability information would actually reduce verification.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Suggests the missing ingredient is calibrated, task-specific reliability/coverage information (X4), not more citations. For energy diligence products: does the product report which checks it ran, which documents it did not cover, and its validated error rates per task type?
analyst_inference: Frames full re-verification as a rational response to unknown error rates (W2-like opacity about the tool's reliability), distinct from W1 obligations; reliability disclosure is a candidate lever but untested here.

proposition_tested: P2.2 Traceability/structured evidence preserves or improves detection of material errors (source grounding reduces fabrication); P2.5.
observed_finding: Per the repository abstract (fetched as a summary, not verbatim): in an RCT, upper-level law students completed legal tasks with a RAG-based legal tool (Vincent AI), a reasoning model (OpenAI o1-preview), or no AI. Both tools improved quality on several tasks and raised productivity in five of six tasks; the reasoning model improved analytical depth, and the RAG tool produced fewer fabricated outputs. Secondary coverage reports the RAG tool's hallucination count was similar to no-AI work, while o1-preview produced more.
evidence_type: direct evidence (randomized controlled trial), seen only via abstract/secondary coverage
population_and_setting: Upper-level law students, U.S. law schools (UMN, Michigan); six legal tasks.
study_or_observation_method: Randomized controlled trial (within-subject task assignment per secondary accounts).
intervention_and_comparator: RAG legal tool vs reasoning model vs no AI.
outcome_measured: Graded quality, time/productivity, hallucinations.
quantitative_result: Abstract (paraphrased by fetch tool): productivity gains roughly 50% to 130% in five of six tasks. Hallucination counts reported in Law360 coverage via search summary (UNVERIFIED): Vincent AI 3, o1-preview 11, no AI 4. Sample size not verified.
source_locator: not located (abstract only)
limitations: Full text blocked; numbers unverified; students not practitioners; grading by researchers, not by supervising lawyers; no measure of supervisory review time. WS7 is separately verifying related Choi et al. statistics.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Suggests grounding in a closed source set reduces fabrication by the producer (W3) but does not by itself show the recipient can check less. Energy diligence analog: a document-grounded assistant vs an ungrounded reasoning model; need recipient-side review-time and error-catch measures.
analyst_inference: Source grounding appears to trade analytical depth for fidelity; neither result speaks to how much the downstream supervisor must re-check.

proposition_tested: P1.1 Retained review is substantially driven by formal obligations that persist regardless of producer transparency.
observed_finding: ABA Formal Opinion 512 states that relying on or submitting GAI output without an appropriate degree of independent verification or review could violate the competence duty (Model Rule 1.1), that the appropriate amount depends on the tool and the specific task, and that supervisory lawyers (Rules 5.1, 5.3) must set policies, train, and make reasonable efforts to ensure compliance, drawing on earlier outsourcing opinions.
population_and_setting: U.S. lawyers subject to ABA Model Rules (as adopted by states).
study_or_observation_method: Formal ethics opinion.
source_locator: Opinion 512, competence (Rule 1.1) discussion and supervision (Rules 5.1/5.3) discussion; original page not located (quoted via Stephens 2024)
short_exact_excerpt: a lawyer’s reliance on, or submission of, a GAI tool’s output—without an appropriate degree of independent verification or review of its output—could violate the duty to provide competent representation as required by Model Rule 1.1.
limitations: Primary text blocked; quotation via secondary source. Advisory, non-binding; does not quantify review.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Analog to credit/IC policies requiring the accountable officer to independently review outside analysis. The obligation is scaled to tool and task, not fixed - so some reduction is permitted where reliability is demonstrated.
analyst_inference: W1 is real but not a fixed quantum: the obligation is to perform 'appropriate' review, leaving room for evidence about tool reliability to change how much is needed.

proposition_tested: P2.4 Visibility into checks performed/validated reliability improves appropriate reliance; P-NEW: prior validation on a sample can substitute for item-level re-review.
observed_finding: Opinion 512 gives an example: a lawyer using GAI to review and summarize many lengthy contracts would not necessarily need to manually review the entire set if the lawyer had previously tested the tool's accuracy on a smaller subset by manual comparison and found the summaries accurate; legal-specific or discrete-task tools may require less verification where prior experience provides a reasonable basis for reliance.
population_and_setting: U.S. lawyers.
study_or_observation_method: Formal ethics opinion.
source_locator: Opinion 512, Rule 1.1 discussion (contract-review example); original page not located (quoted via Stephens 2024 and Roberts 2026)
short_exact_excerpt: the lawyer would not necessarily have to manually review the entire set of documents to verify the results if the lawyer had previously tested the accuracy of the tool on a smaller subset of documents
limitations: No guidance on sample size, error tolerance, matter risk, or revalidation after tool changes (see WS3-E07).
transferability_to_target_workflow: Directly relevant: an accountable reviewer may rely on validated process reliability instead of re-checking every item - the same logic as TAR validation (WS3-E08 to E13). For diligence products, a buyer-run pilot comparing outputs to manual review on a subset is the professional analog.
analyst_inference: The professional standard itself endorses 'verify the process on a sample, then rely' - but places the validation burden on the recipient, not the producer.

proposition_tested: P2.4 (challenge): reliance based on prior experience/validation may not be appropriate when tool behavior is unstable.
observed_finding: The commentator argues Opinion 512's allowance for reduced verification based on prior experience with legal-specific tools is flawed: tools change rapidly so prior experience is not a stable baseline; the opinion's own cited Stanford study reports 17-33% hallucination rates; and the contract-review example omits conditions such as matter risk, document importance, and consequences of a miss. He concludes citations, quotations, holdings and case analysis must be independently verified.
population_and_setting: U.S. legal profession; ABA and Mississippi Bar guidance.
study_or_observation_method: Commentary.
quantitative_result: Cites 17%-33% hallucination rate from Magesh et al. (WS3-S01); no new data.
source_locator: Article body (single web page), paragraphs on 'prior experience' and the contract-review example
short_exact_excerpt: even legal-specific generative AI tools do not justify a lower level of verification for most legal tasks, especially legal research.
limitations: Opinion piece; single author.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Warns that validation-based reduced review requires revalidation when the producer's process changes - relevant to AI-assisted diligence products updated frequently. Verify whether vendors disclose version changes and re-run validation.
analyst_inference: Locates the condition under which X4-style validation stops substituting for item review: non-stationary producers. TAR protocols handle this by validating each production, not relying on past experience.

proposition_tested: P2.4 Visibility into scope/checks performed (process transparency and sampling) supports appropriate reliance without exhaustive item review.
observed_finding: The court approved computer-assisted review for over three million documents based on: the parties' agreement, volume, superiority over linear manual review or keywords, proportionality, and the producing party's transparent protocol. The protocol included a 2,399-document random sample, seven iterative training rounds of at least 500 documents each, a final quality-check random sample of 2,399 documents from the discards, and disclosure to the opposing party of all non-privileged seed-set and training documents with their coding. The court stated that the rules do not require perfection.
evidence_type: court decision (judicial acceptance of process-based validation)
population_and_setting: Employment discrimination class action e-discovery, S.D.N.Y., 2012; adversarial setting with requesting party able to challenge.
study_or_observation_method: Judicial opinion approving ESI protocol.
intervention_and_comparator: Predictive coding with transparent, sampled protocol vs linear manual review or keyword search (as alternatives considered by court).
outcome_measured: Judicial approval / defensibility.
quantitative_result: Collection >3 million documents; random sample 2,399 documents; 7 rounds x >=500 documents; final QC sample 2,399 documents from documents coded non-relevant.
source_locator: ECF Doc. 96, pp. 9-11 (protocol), p. 21 (perfection), p. 22 (five factors), p. 23 (transparency)
short_exact_excerpt: MSL's transparency in its proposed ESI search protocol made it easier for the Court to approve the use of predictive coding.
limitations: Approval tied to this case's protocol and party agreement; does not measure realized recall.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Strong structural analog: producer (responding party/vendor) -> receiving professional (opposing counsel/court) -> decision. Acceptance rests on disclosed process, sampling of what was excluded (checks with no findings), and opportunity to challenge. For diligence: disclose what was reviewed, how, and a sample of what was screened out.
analyst_inference: Shows an institution replacing item-level review with process-plus-sample validation when volume makes exhaustive review impractical and the alternative (manual review) is itself imperfect.

proposition_tested: P-NEW: Outcome and coverage validation (recall/precision, QC sampling) can substitute for a faithful explanation of the producer's internal method.
observed_finding: Judge Peck, quoting his own 2011 article in the opinion, said that in a challenge he would want to know what was done and why it produced defensible results, and might be less interested in the science behind the vendor's 'black box' than in whether it produced responsive documents with reasonably high recall and precision; counsel would not be required to explain why they coded documents, just what the coding was, and proof of a valid process including quality-control testing would be important.
population_and_setting: U.S. federal e-discovery.
study_or_observation_method: Judicial opinion.
source_locator: ECF Doc. 96, pp. 4-5 (quoting Peck, 'Search, Forward', L. Tech. News, Oct. 2011)
short_exact_excerpt: I may be less interested in the science behind the "black box" of the vendor's software than in whether it produced responsive documents with reasonably high recall and high precision.
limitations: Statement of one influential judge's approach; not a binding rule.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Suggests recipients may accept opaque producer reasoning (X2 absent) if coverage and outcome checks (X4 with X5 estimates) are available. For AI diligence: measured completeness of issue-spotting may matter more to reviewers than model explanations.
analyst_inference: Key discriminator for the thesis: the legal system accepted X4/X5 evidence in lieu of X2 explanations - evidence that 'explainability' is not the operative lever for review reduction in this setting.

proposition_tested: P2.4 Coverage/checks visibility (recall estimation, gap analysis, QC of excluded items) lets reviewers verify process without exhaustive review.
observed_finding: Three years after Da Silva Moore, the court stated it is black letter law that courts permit a producing party to use TAR; requesting parties can ensure training and review were done appropriately via statistical estimation of recall at the end of review, checking for gaps in production, and QC review of samples of documents categorized non-responsive; and it is inappropriate to hold TAR to a higher standard than keywords or manual review. The stipulated protocol defined a statistically valid sample as permitting extrapolation with +/-2% margin of error at 95% confidence and used control and validation sets.
population_and_setting: Commercial litigation e-discovery, S.D.N.Y., 2015.
study_or_observation_method: Judicial opinion approving stipulated TAR protocol.
intervention_and_comparator: TAR with validation vs keyword/manual review standards.
outcome_measured: Judicial approval; validation design.
quantitative_result: Protocol: statistically valid sample = margin of error +/-2% at 95% confidence level.
source_locator: ECF Doc. 207, p. 2 (black letter law), p. 6 (alternative validation means; no higher standard), protocol definitions at pp. 10-11 (Doc. 181-1 para. (e))
short_exact_excerpt: requesting parties can insure that training and review was done appropriately by other means, such as statistical estimation of recall at the conclusion of the review
limitations: Validation statements are dicta; the court did not rule on seed-set transparency because the parties agreed a protocol.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Validation targets the recipient's real concern - what was missed - via sampling of the excluded set. Diligence analog: sampling documents/risks the advisor flagged as immaterial or did not review.
analyst_inference: Separates two routes to trust: process transparency (seeing inputs/training) and outcome validation (sampling results). The court treats outcome validation as sufficient even without full process transparency.

proposition_tested: P2.4 (qualification): how much process transparency a reviewer is entitled to is contested.
observed_finding: The court surveyed cases and found that on seed-set transparency 'the decisions are split and the debate in the discovery literature is robust'; some courts required full access to seed sets, others declined to compel disclosure.
population_and_setting: U.S. federal TAR case law to 2015.
study_or_observation_method: Judicial review of precedents.
source_locator: ECF Doc. 207, pp. 4-6
short_exact_excerpt: the decisions are split and the debate in the discovery literature is robust
limitations: Snapshot as of 2015.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Producers resist disclosing internal work (confidentiality, effort); recipients want it. In advisory relationships, what evidence an advisor must expose is a negotiated term, not a given.
analyst_inference: Process transparency carries producer costs and disputes; outcome-based validation was the compromise that let courts avoid the issue.

proposition_tested: P2.2 Structured/validated processes preserve or improve detection while reducing item-level review; P-NEW: exhaustive human item review is not a gold standard.
observed_finding: Using TREC 2009 Legal Track data, the two technology-assisted efforts studied (H5 and Waterloo, five topic-runs) required human review of on average 1.9% of documents and achieved higher average precision and F1 than exhaustive manual review by TREC assessors; average recall was also higher but not statistically significant. No measure showed manual review significantly better.
evidence_type: secondary quantitative analysis of benchmark data
population_and_setting: TREC 2009 Legal Track Interactive Task; ~836,165-document collection; law-student and professional reviewer assessments as manual comparator.
study_or_observation_method: Comparison of recall/precision/F1 against adjudicated gold standard; bootstrap significance tests.
intervention_and_comparator: Technology-assisted review (human-computer interactive) vs exhaustive manual review.
outcome_measured: Recall, precision, F1; share of documents reviewed by humans.
quantitative_result: Table 7 averages: TAR recall 76.7% vs manual 59.3% (difference not significant, P > 0.1); precision 84.7% vs 31.7% (P < 0.001); F1 80.0% vs 36.0% (P < 0.001). TAR human review ~1.9% of documents ('fifty-fold savings'). Manual recall ranged ~25% (Topic 203) to ~80% (Topic 202).
source_locator: Table 7, p. 36-37; para. [47] p. 37; para. [52] p. 43; Conclusion para. [61] p. 48
short_exact_excerpt: The technology-assisted reviews require, on average, human review of only 1.9% of the documents, a fifty-fold savings over exhaustive manual review.
limitations: Best-performing TAR teams selected, not representative TAR; small number of topics; authors' interests; gold-standard construction via appeals may favor participants. Authors stress processes combined human judgment and computers.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism (well-designed process + targeted human judgment can beat exhaustive review on completeness) transfers to high-volume document diligence (lease/title/contract review), less to bespoke judgments like resource or merchant-price assumptions.
analyst_inference: Undercuts the premise that retained exhaustive review buys assurance; much of it may be ritual or habit (P1.6) where volume is large and humans tire. But conditions matter - only good processes beat manual review.

proposition_tested: P1.6 Review persists due to comfort/legitimacy beyond rational verification needs.
observed_finding: The article opens by quoting the Sedona Conference that there 'appears to be a myth' that manual human review is as accurate and complete as possible and the gold standard, and concludes that the myth that exhaustive manual review is the most effective and therefore most defensible approach is strongly refuted; human assessors missed between 20% and 75% of relevant documents.
population_and_setting: E-discovery practice, ca. 2009-2011.
study_or_observation_method: As WS3-E12.
outcome_measured: Recall of manual review.
quantitative_result: Manual review recall approx. 25% to 80% across five topics (human assessors missed 20%-75% of relevant documents).
source_locator: para. [1] p. 2-3 (Sedona quotation); para. [47] p. 37; para. [61] p. 48
short_exact_excerpt: the myth that exhaustive manual review is the most effective – and therefore, the most defensible – approach to document review is strongly refuted.
limitations: Defensibility claim is the authors' interpretation; same selection limits as WS3-E12.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Suggests some recipient re-review in diligence may be defensibility-driven rather than error-catching. Need: data on catch rates of IC/credit re-review of advisor reports.
analyst_inference: Legal profession's attachment to exhaustive review was defended on defensibility grounds; courts shifted once validation evidence offered an alternative defensibility route.

proposition_tested: P1.1 Formal obligations drive retained review - here transformed from item review into a validation obligation; P2.4.
observed_finding: Some courts have held that Rule 26(g)'s 'reasonable inquiry' standard incorporates an obligation for the responding party to validate TAR results, and courts may require validation whether TAR or keyword searches are used; in City of Rockford v. Mallinckrodt the court ordered a random sample of the null set (documents not produced) after keyword searching, with responsive documents found to be produced.
population_and_setting: U.S. federal courts, 2018-2022 decisions.
study_or_observation_method: Case-law review by professional working group.
source_locator: Section on Validation (Part B), p. 33, fns 195-198
short_exact_excerpt: Courts may require validation regardless of whether parties use TAR or keyword searches.
limitations: Secondary summary; underlying decisions not read; public-comment draft superseded.
transferability_to_target_workflow: The accountable party's duty becomes 'show your process found what matters (sample what you excluded)' rather than 'look at everything'. Diligence analog: IC policy could require advisors to report null-set sampling of unreviewed or screened-out material.
analyst_inference: W1 is not necessarily item-level re-performance; governance can be redesigned so the obligation is met by validating coverage.

proposition_tested: P2.4 (conditions): coverage metrics support reliance only with qualitative review of misses, adequate thresholds, and proportionality.
observed_finding: In In re Diisocyanates, the special master held recall estimates of 74-89% reasonable against a 70-80% range the parties called acceptable, but also qualitatively reviewed samples of documents not found, noted that broad recall statistics alone are of limited utility for rare documents, and required some defendants to continue review until batch relevance fell to 10%. In Lawson v. Spirit AeroSystems, ~85% recall was held reasonable and a demand for 100% recall rejected; the TAR effort cost $600,000 and found 3.3% of a 322,000-document set responsive.
population_and_setting: U.S. federal litigation (Diisocyanates antitrust MDL; Lawson v. Spirit AeroSystems), decisions ca. 2020-2022.
study_or_observation_method: Case-law review.
outcome_measured: Judicially accepted recall thresholds and validation practices.
quantitative_result: Diisocyanates: recall 74%-89% accepted vs 70%-80% acceptable range; continue until batch relevance <=10% (last batches were 19% and 15% relevant). Lawson: recall ~85%; cost $600,000; 3.3% of 322,000 documents responsive; initial TAR 2.0 round 68.5% recall.
source_locator: Part B.1 'Role of Recall', pp. 34-36, fns 202-220
short_exact_excerpt: broad validation statistics such as recall, standing alone, are of limited utility in ascertaining whether a party has done a reasonable job of searching for such rare documents.
limitations: Secondary summary; excerpt is the primer quoting the special master (fn 217).
transferability_to_target_workflow: Coverage metrics can mislead for rare, high-impact items - exactly the fatal-flaw issues in project finance diligence (e.g., a single title defect or interconnection condition). Reviewers will need qualitative inspection of what was missed, not just a coverage percentage.
analyst_inference: Conditions for X4 to substitute for item review: explicit acceptable-miss thresholds, sampling of the excluded set, qualitative review of misses, and stopping rules. Rare-but-material items weaken metric-only assurance.

proposition_tested: P2.2 Disclosed underlying evidence enables detection of errors in producer summaries; P3.2 burden can shift to the recipient.
observed_finding: In In re Domestic Airline Travel Antitrust Litigation, the defendant reported TAR validation metrics of 85% recall and 58% precision, but also provided the underlying validation sampling metrics required by the protocol; plaintiffs' analysis of those showed 97.4% recall and 16.7% precision. The defendant acknowledged error; the court said that unless the defendant restarted, plaintiffs must review all the documents, and extended discovery noting 70 attorneys could not finish under existing deadlines.
population_and_setting: Multidistrict antitrust class action (court and date not verified from primary; summarized in primer).
study_or_observation_method: Case-law review.
outcome_measured: Detection of erroneous validation summary; burden consequence.
quantitative_result: Reported: recall 85%, precision 58%. Recomputed from validation sample: recall 97.4%, precision 16.7%. 70 attorneys engaged in receiving-side review.
source_locator: Part B.2 'Role of Precision', pp. 36-37, fns 221-225
short_exact_excerpt: they found that the statistics from the validation sample indicated that the TAR process resulted in a recall of 97.4% and precision of 16.7%
limitations: Single case via secondary summary.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Disclosure of the raw check data (not just the producer's summary metric) let the recipient catch a summary error - supports requiring diligence products to expose the underlying sample/evidence behind headline conclusions. Also shows over-inclusive producer output shifts review volume to recipients.
analyst_inference: Best single illustration in WS3 that X4 + X3 at the level of underlying data can improve error detection (P2.2), and that a producer optimizing one metric (recall) can push cost onto the recipient (P3.2).

proposition_tested: P1.1 Formal obligations require the accountable professional to verify regardless of the producer; P1.3 producer errors.
observed_finding: The court stated there is nothing inherently improper about using a reliable AI tool, but existing rules impose a gatekeeping role on attorneys to ensure the accuracy of filings (Rule 11). Respondents abandoned their responsibilities by submitting non-existent opinions with fake quotes and citations generated by ChatGPT and standing by them after challenge. The court listed harms (opposing party's time and money, court's time, client harm, reputational harm) and imposed a $5,000 penalty jointly and severally.
population_and_setting: U.S. federal personal-injury case, S.D.N.Y., 2023.
study_or_observation_method: Sanctions opinion.
outcome_measured: Sanction.
quantitative_result: $5,000 penalty, jointly and severally on respondents; also ordered letters to the client and to each judge falsely identified as author of a fake opinion.
source_locator: ECF Doc. 54, pp. 1-2 (gatekeeping; harms), pp. 33-34 (penalty and letters to client and judges)
short_exact_excerpt: nothing inherently improper about using a reliable artificial intelligence tool for assistance. But existing rules impose a gatekeeping role on attorneys to ensure the accuracy of their filings.
limitations: Extreme facts; bad faith turned partly on post-challenge conduct.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Analog: the IC/credit officer who signs off bears the gatekeeping duty for facts in the memo regardless of who drafted them. Diligence products cannot remove this W1 element; they can only make it cheaper to discharge.
analyst_inference: Gatekeeping is non-delegable; the question for the thesis is cost of discharging it, not whether it exists.

proposition_tested: P1.1 Supervising signer must perform own inquiry; reliance on another professional's work does not discharge it.
observed_finding: The signing attorney (LoDuca) filed an affirmation drafted with research by a colleague (Schwartz); the court found he violated Rule 11 by not reading a single cited case and taking no other step to check whether the legal assertions were warranted, aggravated by knowing the colleague's unfamiliarity with the area and the firm's research-tool limits. Each respondent's knowledge and conduct is assessed separately; imputation of knowledge does not apply.
population_and_setting: As WS3-E17.
study_or_observation_method: Sanctions opinion.
source_locator: ECF Doc. 54, pp. 29-30, paras. 22-23
short_exact_excerpt: Mr. LoDuca violated Rule 11 in not reading a single case cited in his March 1 Affirmation in Opposition and taking no other steps on his own to check whether any aspect of the assertions of law were warranted
limitations: The court noted an inadequate inquiry may not be bad faith; the violation was making no inquiry at all. Does not specify the minimum adequate inquiry.
transferability_to_target_workflow: The producer here is a human colleague, not AI - closest legal analog to a recipient relying on an outside advisor's work. Standard: the signer must take some own steps, scaled to known weaknesses of the producer.
analyst_inference: Retained review is calibrated to what the recipient knows about the producer's competence; information about producer limits raises required inquiry - transparency can increase, not just decrease, required checking.

proposition_tested: P1.3 Producer inaccuracy drives the need for review; P2.5 citations to real sources can misrepresent them.
observed_finding: The database lists 2,293 decisions (as of access) in which a court or tribunal found or implied reliance on hallucinated content. Filter counts: USA 1,554; party type Lawyer 913, Pro Se Litigant 1,315, Judge 34, Expert 18; nature Fabricated 1,877, Misrepresented 971, False Quotes 607, Outdated Advice 38 (categories overlap).
evidence_type: compiled database of court decisions (observed sanctions/findings)
population_and_setting: Court and tribunal decisions worldwide, Q2 2023 to Nov 2026.
study_or_observation_method: Curated compilation by one researcher.
outcome_measured: Count of decisions addressing hallucinated material.
quantitative_result: 2,293 decisions total; Lawyer 913; Pro Se 1,315; Fabricated 1,877; Misrepresented 971; False Quotes 607 (filter counts on landing page, 2026-11-15).
source_locator: Landing page header and filter panel
short_exact_excerpt: It does not track the (necessarily wider) universe of all fake citations or use of AI in court filings.
limitations: No denominator; detection depends on opponents/courts catching errors; curator discretion.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Shows realized consequences of under-verification at scale in a profession with explicit verification duties; 'misrepresented' (real source, wrong claim) category is the citation-correctness gap most relevant to source-linked diligence outputs.
analyst_inference: Hundreds of lawyer cases despite clear duties suggest time pressure leads some professionals to skip verification - evidence that verification cost is binding, not merely ritual.

proposition_tested: P1.1 Retained review is required by governance regardless of transparency; challenges P2.1 within this regime (designer's calculations deliberately withheld from the checker).
observed_finding: For technical approval of UK highway structures, the checker's analytical models and work must be independent of the designer's and carried out without exchange of calculation sheets or similar analytical work; the two may consult to ensure results are comparable, and the method of analysis need not be the same. The checker must comprehensively examine all aspects and check that calculations are accurately translated into details and drawings.
evidence_type: professional standard (mandatory requirement for UK trunk-road structures)
population_and_setting: UK highway structures under National Highways/Overseeing Organisations; Technical Approval Authority (TAA) process.
study_or_observation_method: Standard text.
source_locator: CG 300 v0.2.1, Section 2 'Checking procedure', clauses 2.69, 2.70, 2.74, 2.74.1 (and NOTE), 2.75
short_exact_excerpt: The Checker's analytical models and analytical work shall be independent of that of the Designer or Assessor and carried out without exchange of calculation sheets, or similar analytical work, between the Designer or Assessor and the Checker.
limitations: Obligation, not evidence of effectiveness or cost.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Where governance values an independent second derivation (to catch common-mode errors and anchoring), traceability to the producer's working is intentionally restricted and reconstruction is the point. Analog: independent re-modeling of energy yield (P50/P90) by a lender's IE. Verify where in energy diligence lenders demand independent re-derivation vs review of the sponsor's model.
analyst_inference: Strongest counterexample to 'traceability always reduces avoidable reconstruction': for high-complexity items, re-derivation is W1 by design, and sharing producer workings could undermine independence. Results-level comparison (2.74.1) is the permitted linkage.

proposition_tested: P-NEW: Governance scales the independence/intensity of re-derivation to complexity and novelty rather than requiring it uniformly.
observed_finding: CG 300 grades checking: categories 0 and 1 are checked independently by another engineer who may be from the design team; category 2 by a check team from the same organisation but independent of the design team; category 3 by a check team from a separate organisation proposed by the designer and agreed by the TAA. Category 3 covers complex structures requiring sophisticated analysis or with features such as high redundancy, novel design, any span over 50 m, skew over 45 degrees, difficult foundations, or movable bridges.
population_and_setting: As WS3-E20.
study_or_observation_method: Standard text.
quantitative_result: Category 3 thresholds include span > 50 m and skew > 45 degrees.
source_locator: CG 300 v0.2.1, Section 2 'Checking procedure' list items 1)-3); Section 3 'Category 3' clause (number not pinned)
short_exact_excerpt: category 3 are checked by a check team from a separate organisation proposed by the Designer or Assessor and agreed by the TAA.
limitations: As WS3-E20.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Suggests a risk-tiered model for recipient review of advisor work: routine items checked lightly, novel/complex items independently re-derived. Diligence analog: standard lease review vs novel hybrid storage revenue models.
analyst_inference: W1 intensity is itself a design variable tied to novelty and consequence; a product could target the low/medium tiers where evidence linkage plausibly substitutes, while leaving top-tier independent re-derivation intact.

proposition_tested: P1.1 Independent design verification by persons other than the designer is a formal requirement.
observed_finding: Appendix B Criterion III requires design control measures that provide for verifying or checking design adequacy, such as by design reviews, alternate or simplified calculational methods, or a suitable testing program, performed by individuals or groups other than those who performed the original design (who may be from the same organization).
population_and_setting: U.S. nuclear power and fuel reprocessing plant licensees and their contractors; safety-related structures, systems, components.
study_or_observation_method: Regulatory text.
source_locator: 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, Criterion III (Design Control)
short_exact_excerpt: The verifying or checking process shall be performed by individuals or groups other than those who performed the original design, but who may be from the same organization.
limitations: Obligation only; the choice among review, alternate calculation, or testing is left to the licensee.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Shows menu-based verification: design review (checking the work as presented) is an accepted alternative to re-derivation (alternate calculation). Diligence analog: credit teams may verify a model by review or by independent simplified recalculation.
analyst_inference: Even in nuclear QA, re-derivation is one option, not mandated - so 'review of documented work' (where traceability helps) is formally acceptable verification.

proposition_tested: P-NEW: Acceptance of outsourced work may rest on supplier-furnished objective evidence plus periodic assessment of the supplier's quality system, graded by importance, rather than re-performance; relates to P2.4.
observed_finding: Criterion VII requires measures to assure purchased material, equipment and services conform to procurement documents, including as appropriate source evaluation and selection, objective evidence of quality furnished by the contractor, inspection at source, and examination on delivery; documentary evidence of conformance must be available and retained; the effectiveness of contractors' quality control is to be assessed at intervals consistent with the importance, complexity and quantity of the product or services.
population_and_setting: As WS3-E22; applies to purchased services including outside engineering.
study_or_observation_method: Regulatory text.
source_locator: 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, Criterion VII (Control of Purchased Material, Equipment, and Services)
short_exact_excerpt: objective evidence of quality furnished by the contractor or subcontractor, inspection at the contractor or subcontractor source, and examination of products upon delivery.
limitations: Obligation only; no data on how much re-checking occurs in practice.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Closest regulatory analog to the thesis: the buyer accepts outside work using the supplier's documented evidence and periodic audits of the supplier's process, graded by importance. Diligence analog: lenders accepting IE work based on IE qualification and documented scope rather than redoing it.
analyst_inference: Supports a two-level design: evidence-of-quality per deliverable (X3) plus periodic supplier-process assessment (X4), with intensity graded by consequence.

proposition_tested: P1.1 Independent review is required where judgment exceeds prescriptive rules; responsibility is not transferred by review.
observed_finding: The guidelines require independent peer review for performance-based tall-building design because such design entails judgments outside prescriptive requirements; most building departments require it and ASCE 7 includes it; the authors recommend using the guidelines for approval only with independent third-party review. The Engineer of Record remains solely responsible; peer review does not relieve design responsibility and is not intended to replace the EOR's own QA, although in many cases it effectively constitutes the plan review of the seismic system.
population_and_setting: Performance-based seismic design of tall buildings (U.S. West Coast practice).
study_or_observation_method: Consensus guideline.
source_locator: PEER 2017/06 v2.03, Section 8.1 and commentary (p. 8-1); Section 8.5 and commentary (p. 8-4)
short_exact_excerpt: Peer review participation is not intended to replace quality assurance measures ordinarily exercised by the Engineer of Record.
limitations: Guidance; does not quantify review effort or effectiveness.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Producer (EOR) -> independent reviewer -> authority (building official) -> public consequence structure mirrors sponsor -> IE/advisor -> lender. Independent review is triggered by departure from prescriptive rules - analog: non-standard project structures trigger heavier lender review.
analyst_inference: Layered review is designed redundancy (producer QA + independent review + authority plan review); W1 here is structural, so transparency could reduce cost per layer but not remove layers.

proposition_tested: P2.4 Visibility into key assumptions and agreed criteria improves review efficiency; P1.2 avoidable reconstruction from poorly presented evidence; P-NEW: more raw evidence is not better.
observed_finding: The guidelines direct designers to present documentation to facilitate efficient transfer to peer reviewers: highlight assumptions with substantial effect and departures from standard practice; interpret results and validate assumptions; provide key results with explanations of what they mean rather than binders of raw analysis data; accompany key spreadsheets with fully worked examples; and agree a Basis of Design early, which becomes the set of rules against which subsequent design and analyses are checked.
population_and_setting: As WS3-E24.
study_or_observation_method: Consensus guideline commentary.
source_locator: PEER 2017/06 v2.03, Section 7.2 commentary (p. 7-1); Section 7.3 and commentary (pp. 7-1 to 7-2); Section 8.4 commentary (p. 8-3)
short_exact_excerpt: More is not necessarily better. For example, presenting graphical results of key maximum response quantities with explanations of "what it means" is far more effective than submitting binders or computer-storage media full of raw analysis data.
limitations: Expert recommendation, not measured effect.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Directly supports curated evidence linkage (key assumptions flagged, criteria agreed upfront, interpretive summaries with worked examples) over data dumps. Energy diligence analog: agreeing the IC's acceptance criteria (Basis of Design) with the advisor before work starts.
analyst_inference: Distinguishes good traceability (prioritized, interpreted, tied to agreed criteria) from raw provenance volume; the agreed-criteria step is a W4 mechanism (adapting to recipient criteria up front).

proposition_tested: P1.2 A material share of reviewer effort is understanding/reconstructing context and rationale.
observed_finding: Understanding the change and its context emerged as the main challenge of code review; a tester said understanding the code takes most of the reviewing time; clarification questions about rationale were the second most frequent comment category; 91% of surveyed programmers said reviewing unfamiliar files takes longer, and 82% said reviewers familiar with the files give different (deeper, more conceptual) feedback; descriptions are considered good when they state what was changed and why.
evidence_type: observational field study (interviews, comment content analysis, surveys)
population_and_setting: Microsoft developers using CodeFlow; 17 observed/interviewed; 570 review comments; surveys of 165 managers and 873 programmers.
study_or_observation_method: Mixed methods: observation, interviews, card sort, surveys.
outcome_measured: Self-reported challenges; comment categories.
quantitative_result: 798 of programmers (91%) said unfamiliar files take longer to review; 716 (82%) said familiar reviewers give different feedback; manager survey 165 responses (28% response rate); programmer survey 873.
source_locator: Section VI.A 'Code Review is Understanding' and VI.B; Abstract
short_exact_excerpt: understanding the code takes most of the reviewing time.
limitations: Self-report; single company; no timing measurement; quote is one participant.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Reviewer cost is dominated by building context and grasping rationale - the W2 component the thesis targets. Diligence analog: IC members unfamiliar with a project spend effort reconstructing why the advisor concluded X. Verify by timing reviewers with vs without rationale/assumption summaries.
analyst_inference: Most direct engineering evidence that rationale/context access drives review cost; but familiarity (reviewer expertise) also changes review quality, so cost reduction via summaries may also reduce depth.

proposition_tested: P1.6 Review persists for reasons beyond error detection (knowledge transfer, awareness).
observed_finding: Although finding defects is the top stated motivation, defect comments were only the fourth most frequent category (78 of 570 comments, 14%), mostly about low-level logic; code improvements were most frequent (165, 29%). Review also delivered knowledge transfer, team awareness, and alternative solutions.
population_and_setting: As WS3-E26.
study_or_observation_method: Card sort of 570 comments from 200 review threads.
outcome_measured: Comment category frequencies.
quantitative_result: Defects 78/570 (14%); code improvements 165/570 (29%); knowledge-transfer comments 12.
source_locator: Section V (outcomes), Figure 4
short_exact_excerpt: Review comments about defects are few, comprising one-eighth of the total in our sample
limitations: Comment counts understate non-written outcomes; single company.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Recipient review of advisor work in investment firms may also serve learning, ownership and shared understanding for the decision; cutting review to save time may lose those functions. Need: whether IC members value re-review for understanding rather than error catching.
analyst_inference: Not all retained review is verification; some is how decision-makers internalize the analysis they must defend - relevant to whether 'less review' is desirable.

proposition_tested: P2.4 Visibility into automated checks performed, small scoped changes, and reviewer familiarity are associated with lightweight review (correlational); P1.1 mandatory review persists.
observed_finding: At Google, every change must be approved by a directory owner and by someone with language 'readability' certification; even owners must have code reviewed. Review is lightweight: median one reviewer, fewer than 25% of changes have more than one reviewer, median change 24 lines, median overall review latency under 4 hours, over 80% of changes need at most one iteration. Automatic analyzer results are shown to authors and reviewers in the review tool; reviewer suggestion prioritizes those who recently edited/reviewed the files.
population_and_setting: Google engineers; ~9 million reviewed changes over two years; 12 interviews; survey of 44.
study_or_observation_method: Log analysis plus qualitative interviews and survey.
intervention_and_comparator: Descriptive comparison with other companies (AMD, Microsoft, Chrome OS) from prior literature.
outcome_measured: Review latency, change size, reviewer count, iterations.
quantitative_result: Median reviewers = 1; <25% of changes >1 reviewer; median lines modified = 24; median review latency <4 hours (vs 14.7-24 hours median approval times reported elsewhere); >80% of changes <=1 iteration; ~35% change one file, ~90% fewer than 10 files.
source_locator: Review-process section ('Ownership', 'Readability', 'Code Review Flow', Finding 3) and quantitative review-practice analysis (Finding 4)
short_exact_excerpt: even directory owners are expected to have their code reviewed before committing.
limitations: No causal identification; defect escape not measured; Google-specific tooling and culture.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Suggests review cost falls when work arrives in small, well-scoped units with machine-check results attached and reviewed by people with context - not when review is removed. Diligence analog: modular findings with attached check results routed to the relevant specialist.
analyst_inference: Mandatory review (W1) coexists with low per-item review cost; supports 'make review cheaper' over 'eliminate review'. Weak evidence for P2.4 because associations only.

proposition_tested: P1.6 / P1.1 Review serves gatekeeping, norms and education, not only defect finding.
observed_finding: Code review at Google was introduced primarily to improve code understandability and maintainability (education) rather than to find bugs; developers' expectations comprise education, maintaining norms, gatekeeping, and accident prevention; defect finding is welcomed but not the only focus.
population_and_setting: As WS3-E28.
study_or_observation_method: Interviews (incl. early-history interview) and survey confirmation.
outcome_measured: Stated motivations.
source_locator: RQ1 motivations section, Finding 1
short_exact_excerpt: Defect finding is welcomed but not the only focus.
limitations: Stated motivations; small interview/survey samples.
transferability_to_target_workflow: As WS3-E27: in investment governance, review is also gatekeeping and norm enforcement (policy compliance, W4), not only error detection.
analyst_inference: Corroborates WS3-E27 from a different firm: a large part of retained review is designed governance and socialization, which evidence linkage will not remove.

proposition_tested: P2.1 Access to sources/provenance reduces verification time/effort (tested: retrieved source passages vs LLM explanation)
observed_finding: Showing retrieved Wikipedia passages and showing ChatGPT explanations produced statistically indistinguishable overall human fact-checking accuracy, but reading passages took about 2.5x longer per claim than reading the explanation.
population_and_setting: 80 Prolific crowdworkers (16 per condition), 20 adversarial FoolMeTwice claims each, 1500 judgments
study_or_observation_method: Five conditions (baseline, retrieval, explanation, contrastive explanation, retrieval+explanation); accuracy and time per claim recorded; t-tests
intervention_and_comparator: Top-10 retrieved Wikipedia passages (X3) vs ChatGPT natural-language explanation (X1) vs no assistance
outcome_measured: Binary verification accuracy; minutes per claim
quantitative_result: Accuracy: explanation 0.74 +/- 0.09 vs retrieval 0.73 +/- 0.12 (z = -0.48, p = 0.32); baseline (no evidence) 0.59 +/- 0.12 (explanation vs baseline z = -4.08, p = 0.00015). Time: retrieval 2.53 +/- 1.07 min vs explanation 1.01 +/- 0.45 min per claim (z = -5.09, p = 9.1e-6).
source_locator: Section 5.1 (RQ1 results), Figure 2
short_exact_excerpt: Showing explanations allows significantly faster decision time than showing retrieved passages
limitations: Crowdworkers; Wikipedia sources; condition n=16; time differences may reflect skimming rather than verification.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism (how source access vs AI narrative changes checking time and error catch) plausibly transfers to a diligence reviewer checking an advisor's claims against data-room documents. Consequential differences: lay crowdworkers, no accountability, short binary items, no professional priors; diligence claims are multi-document and judgment-laden. Needs verification with professional reviewers on realistic advisor memos.
analyst_inference: Raw source access is the slower path; the time saving offered by AI narratives is real but (see E02) is bought with loss of error detection when the narrative is wrong. Traceability did not reduce effort relative to a narrative summary here.

proposition_tested: P2.3 Explanations increase acceptance without improving (or while worsening) error detection; P2.2 traceability preserves detection
