study_or_observation_method: Accuracy split by AI-correct vs AI-incorrect items (Figure 4B); qualitative coding of 409 free-text strategy responses.
intervention_and_comparator: Explain-Top-1 vs Conf vs other explanation conditions.
outcome_measured: Accuracy on AI-correct vs AI-incorrect items; self-reported strategies.
quantitative_result: Point estimates for split accuracies shown graphically only (Figure 4B, 95% CIs), not tabulated in text. Self-reports: 'Mostly Follow AI' 23 (6%); 'AI as Prior Guide' 190 (47%); 'AI as Post Check' 102 (25%); 'Mostly Ignore AI' 90 (22%); 'Fall Back to AI' 54 (13%) (Table 3).
source_locator: Figure 4B caption, p. 8; Section 5.1, p. 8; Table 3, p. 11; Section 6.2, p. 12.
short_exact_excerpt: One concerning observation was that explanations increased blind trust rather than appropriate reliance on AI.
limitations: Split-by-correctness results are presented graphically; not all splits significant; lay participants.
transferability_to_target_workflow: The discriminating design (outcomes split by whether the advice was right or wrong) is directly reusable for evaluating advisor-output formats in diligence: seed known errors in advisor reports and measure detection, not overall agreement.
analyst_inference: Shows why 'users accepted more' or 'agreed more' is not evidence of better verification.

proposition_tested: P2.1 Access to explanations/evidence reduces verification effort (qualified: depends on task-specific cost of verifying).
observed_finding: Among participants who mentioned using explanations, 27% (Beer) and 32% (Amzbook) said they used them to read faster; 17% (Beer/Amzbook) reported using explanations to validate AI decisions vs 2% in LSAT, which the authors attribute to LSAT being harder so that verifying explanations is costlier. Authors did not measure speed objectively.
evidence_type: self-reported strategies from experiment exit survey
population_and_setting: As WS7-E08.
study_or_observation_method: Qualitative coding of free-text responses.
outcome_measured: Self-reported use of explanations (speed reading, validation).
quantitative_result: 27% (Beer), 32% (Amzbook) of explanation-mentioning participants used explanations to read faster; 17% (Beer/Amzbook) vs 2% (LSAT) used them to validate the AI.
source_locator: Section 5 qualitative-findings paragraph 'Explanations can help participants validate the AI's decisions...', p. 12; Section 6.1 Limitations, p. 12.
short_exact_excerpt: This could be because LSAT is a harder task than sentiment analysis, and verifying AI’s explanations is costlier.
limitations: Stated behavior, not observed timing; denominators are subsets of coded responses.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: explanation benefit depends on whether checking the explanation is cheaper than redoing the task. In diligence, a source link to a contract clause or meter dataset may be cheap to check; a narrative rationale for a degradation assumption may not be.
analyst_inference: Consistent with the verification-cost account later tested by Vasconcelos et al. (WS7-E21).

proposition_tested: P-NEW: Lay-participant human-AI experiments have limited transferability to expert, high-stakes reliance.
observed_finding: Authors state they restricted themselves to crowdsourcable tasks, results may not generalize to high-stakes domains with expert users, and the effectiveness of explanations may depend on user expertise, which they did not explore. They also evaluated only accuracy, not speed or effort.
population_and_setting: As WS7-E08.
study_or_observation_method: Limitations section.
source_locator: Section 6.1 Limitations, p. 12.
short_exact_excerpt: our results may not generalize to high-stakes domains with expert users such as medical diagnosis.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Lowers the evidentiary weight of this study for RQ2 in renewable diligence; use as mechanism hypothesis only.

proposition_tested: P2.3 Simple explanations do not prevent (and coexist with) overreliance; designs forcing engagement improve error detection.
observed_finding: On items where the simulated AI was wrong, cognitive forcing designs (on-demand, update, wait) produced more correct decisions than simple explainable-AI designs (explanation, explanation+uncertainty), but participants in BOTH AI categories performed worse than unassisted participants on the same items. Across all items, both AI categories outperformed no-AI with no difference between them.
population_and_setting: US MTurk adults; N=199 analysed (260 recruited); nutrition task: replace the highest-carb ingredient in a meal photo with a low-carb, flavor-similar substitute; 26 questions in 2 blocks, 6 with incorrect AI.
study_or_observation_method: Mixed-effects models (participant random effect), Holm-Bonferroni post-hoc t-tests; chi-square on decision distributions.
intervention_and_comparator: Cognitive forcing functions (CFF) vs simple explainable AI (SXAI) vs no AI.
outcome_measured: Overall correctness; carb-source detection; overreliance = % agreement with AI when AI incorrect.
quantitative_result: Incorrect-AI items, marginal means (SE): overall correct - no AI 0.18 (0.02), SXAI 0.03 (0.02), CFF 0.09 (0.01), F(2,261.7)=12.59, p<<.0001, CFF vs SXAI d=.37. Carb-source detection - no AI 0.49 (0.04), SXAI 0.08 (0.03), CFF 0.27 (0.03), F(2,242.6)=35.59, d=.66. Overreliance on carb source: SXAI 0.64 (0.03) vs CFF 0.48 (0.03), F(1,145.8)=9.24, p=.003, d=.36; overall overreliance SXAI 0.30 vs CFF 0.26, n.s. All items, overall correct: no AI 0.17, SXAI 0.35, CFF 0.33 (CFF vs SXAI d=.03).
source_locator: Section 3.5 Participants p. 8-9; Table 1 p. 10; Table 2 and Section 4.1 p. 11.
short_exact_excerpt: cognitive forcing significantly reduced overreliance compared to the simple explainable AI approaches. However, there was a trade-off: people assigned the least favorable subjective ratings to the designs that reduced the overreliance the most.
limitations: Lay participants, non-critical task, simulated AI with salient designed errors; no objective time/effort measure; AI error rate 25% of scored items.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: forcing independent judgment before or alongside advice (e.g., reviewer forms own view of key assumptions before reading advisor conclusion) improves error catching relative to passive acceptance. Diligence analogues: independent model checks, 'red-flag first' review. Difference: professional reviewers with accountability may already engage more; error base rates in advisor reports are unknown.
analyst_inference: Key counterevidence for 'cheaper and no worse': even the best AI-assist designs underperformed the unassisted baseline on wrong-advice items, so overall gains depend on advisor error rates. Also implies that design choices that reduce effort may increase uncaught errors.

proposition_tested: P2.3 Trust/preference diverge from (and here correlate negatively with) appropriate reliance.
observed_finding: Self-reported trust was higher (n.s.) and system complexity significantly lower for simple explainable AI than cognitive forcing; preference for AI-assisted designs over no AI was significant. Trust and preference were significantly negatively correlated with performance on incorrect AI predictions; trust was positively correlated with reliance on incorrect predictions for carb-source detection. Benefits of cognitive forcing were larger for participants high in Need for Cognition.
evidence_type: randomized online experiment, subjective measures and correlations
population_and_setting: As WS7-E12.
study_or_observation_method: 5-point Likert items; Pearson correlations with performance.
intervention_and_comparator: CFF vs SXAI vs no AI.
outcome_measured: Trust, preference, mental demand, complexity; correlation with performance.
quantitative_result: Trust marginal means: SXAI 3.91 (0.09) vs CFF 3.72 (0.08), F(1,146.4)=2.84, n.s. Preference: no AI 3.13 < CFF 3.62, SXAI 3.78, F(2,169.5)=10.52, p<<.0001. System complexity: SXAI < CFF, no AI, F(2,172.2)=6.19, p=.002. Correlation coefficients for trust/preference vs performance reported in figures (e.g., r=-.24, p=.0003 for one NFC-related panel) - not all extracted.
source_locator: Table 3 and Section 4.2, pp. 11-12; Section 5 (Need for Cognition) pp. 12-13; Limitations p. 17.
short_exact_excerpt: Trust and preference were significantly negatively correlated with both overall performance and carb source detection performance for incorrect model predictions.
limitations: Single-item subjective scales; lay task.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Warns that buyer satisfaction with an advisor product that 'feels easier' is not evidence of better verification; designs that preserve scrutiny may be less liked, with adoption implications (RQ6). Needs testing with professional buyers whose incentives include accountability.
analyst_inference: Measurement implication: satisfaction/NPS-type outcomes cannot discriminate cheaper-and-no-worse verification from increased trust.

proposition_tested: P3.3 Drafting is separable from substantive judgment and most amenable to reduction (qualified: speed gains large, quality gains small/inconsistent).
observed_finding: Randomized controlled trial: law students were randomly assigned to complete realistic legal tasks with or without GPT-4 (after training), with time tracked and outputs blind-graded. GPT-4 access only slightly and inconsistently improved quality but produced large, consistent speed increases; where quality improved, lowest-skilled participants benefited most; time savings were roughly uniform across baseline speed; participants reported more satisfaction and correctly guessed which tasks GPT-4 helped most.
population_and_setting: 60 University of Minnesota Law School students (per SSRN abstract, WS7-S06); four tasks: drafting a complaint, a contract, a section of an employee handbook, and a client memo.
study_or_observation_method: Randomized assignment with/without GPT-4 per task; blind grading; timing; follow-up surveys.
intervention_and_comparator: GPT-4 access (with training) vs no AI.
outcome_measured: Task completion time; blind-graded quality; self-reported satisfaction.
quantitative_result: Not available from accessed material. A news report (WS7-S07) states time savings of 12%-32% depending on task; not verified against the paper.
source_locator: Abstract on repository landing page (scholarship.law.umn.edu/minnlrev/vol109/iss1/3/); full text not accessed.
short_exact_excerpt: We found that access to GPT-4 only slightly and inconsistently improved the quality of participants’ legal analysis but induced large and consistent increases in speed.
limitations: Abstract only; students not practitioners; the AI was a drafting aid for the participant's own work product, not an outside advisor's analysis being reviewed; no measure of error detection in someone else's work; graders assessed quality of final product (errors introduced by AI and caught/missed not separately reported in abstract).
transferability_to_target_workflow: Supports a narrow mechanism relevant to RQ3/W5: AI assistance in producing decision documents (e.g., IC memo drafting) can reduce time without degrading graded quality. Does NOT establish that recipients can verify an outside advisor's analysis faster without loss. Not an advisor-client structure.
analyst_inference: Speed vs quality dissociation: time savings are not evidence of quality improvement; useful as an example of measuring both separately.

proposition_tested: P-NEW: The human-AI decision-making evidence base rarely studies domain experts, limiting transferability to professional reliance.
observed_finding: Survey of >100 empirical human-subject studies of AI-assisted decision making: although many decision tasks require domain expertise, experts are seldom the study subjects; many studies of expertise-requiring tasks use crowdworkers, and it is unclear whether results generalize to judges or doctors. Expertise required is often correlated with task risk; low-stakes tasks may not create the vulnerability needed to study trust.
population_and_setting: Published empirical studies (CHI, CSCW, IUI, FAccT, ML venues etc.) through 2021.
study_or_observation_method: Coding of design choices: decision tasks, AI assistance elements, evaluation metrics.
outcome_measured: Distribution of study design choices.
quantitative_result: Not extracted (passages are qualitative).
source_locator: arXiv v1, Section 3 'Decision tasks', pdf pp. 8-9 (task risk/expertise paragraphs and summary of gaps).
short_exact_excerpt: Although many decision tasks require domain expertise, experts are seldom the subjects of study.
limitations: arXiv precursor version, not the FAccT 2023 final; no counts of expert-participant studies extracted.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Primary transferability caution for RQ2: most reliance/explanation findings come from lay participants on low-stakes tasks, unlike credit officers or IC members reviewing IE reports under accountability.
analyst_inference: Absence of expert studies is a gap, not evidence that effects differ for experts; direction of bias is unknown (experts may detect more errors, but Dratsch WS7-E24 shows experts remain susceptible).

proposition_tested: P-NEW: Human-AI decision studies emphasize accuracy and under-measure efficiency/effort, so evidence on 'verification got cheaper' is thin.
observed_finding: The survey identifies efficiency (speed) as a secondary metric; the most common objective efficiency metric is time on task; a stated gap is the focus on decision efficacy with less emphasis on efficiency and user satisfaction.
population_and_setting: As WS7-E15.
study_or_observation_method: Coding of evaluation metrics.
outcome_measured: Metrics used in studies.
source_locator: arXiv v1, Section 5 'Evaluation metrics', 'Efficiency' paragraph, pdf p. 24; 'Gaps in current practices' item (1), pdf p. 28.
short_exact_excerpt: A focus on decision efficacy (i.e., performance), and less emphasis on efficiency and user satisfaction.
limitations: As WS7-E15.
transferability_to_target_workflow: RQ2 needs joint measurement of effort (time, actions, documents opened) and detection quality; the general literature rarely provides both, so target-domain studies must be designed to do so.

proposition_tested: P2.4/P2.3 measurement: a two-dimensional reliance metric can separate 'relying more' from 'relying appropriately'.
observed_finding: Proposes Appropriateness of Reliance (AoR) with two dimensions measured in a sequential design (human decides first, then sees advice): Relative AI Reliance (RAIR: share of initially-wrong cases where the person correctly switches to correct AI advice) and Relative Self-Reliance (RSR: share of initially-correct cases where the person correctly rejects wrong AI advice). Feature-importance explanations increased RAIR without significantly reducing RSR; however, human-AI team accuracy was not significantly different from human-alone accuracy.
population_and_setting: 200 Prolific participants (1 excluded); deceptive vs genuine hotel review classification; 16 main items stratified 4 per confusion-matrix cell (AI accuracy 50% on main items).
study_or_observation_method: Between-subjects (AI advice only vs AI advice + feature-importance explanation); t-tests; structural equation model.
intervention_and_comparator: Explanations (feature-importance highlights) vs advice only.
outcome_measured: RAIR, RSR, accuracy, confidence change, trust.
quantitative_result: RAIR 29.59% (+/-3pp) control vs 38.87% (+/-3pp) XAI, t=-1.95, p=0.05; RSR 71.87% (+/-3pp) vs 69.45% (+/-3pp), t=0.61, p=0.54. Team performance not significantly different from human accuracy (complementary performance not reached).
source_locator: Section 3 (AoR definition) pp. 6-7; Section 4 participants p. 12; Section 5 results p. 14 (Fig. 6) and p. 15.
short_exact_excerpt: It is important to highlight that RAIR is not increased simply by relying more often on AI advice, as this would have also reduced the RSR significantly. [math-italic glyphs rendered as plain letters]
limitations: Lay participants; near-chance task; artificial 50% AI accuracy; p=0.05 borderline; no effort measure.
transferability_to_target_workflow: The measurement design transfers: in diligence studies, have reviewers form an initial view on a set of advisor findings (some seeded wrong), then reveal advisor output in different formats; measure RAIR-like (correctly adopting correct findings) and RSR-like (correctly rejecting wrong findings) rates plus time.
analyst_inference: Provides the core discriminating metric for 'trusted more' (RAIR up, RSR down) vs 'verified better' (RAIR up, RSR flat or up).

proposition_tested: P-NEW: Receiving decision support raises the risk of adopting its errors (commission errors) relative to unaided decisions.
observed_finding: Small indicative meta-analysis of four healthcare CDSS studies: erroneous advice was more likely to be followed in CDSS groups than in controls; when in error, CDSS increased the risk of an incorrect decision by 26%.
population_and_setting: Healthcare clinical decision support users (4 pooled studies); review covers 74 studies across healthcare, aviation, generic settings, all expertise levels.
study_or_observation_method: Mantel-Haenszel random-effects risk ratio (RevMan).
intervention_and_comparator: CDSS with erroneous advice vs no-CDSS control.
outcome_measured: Erroneous decisions following incorrect advice.
quantitative_result: Risk ratio 1.26 (95% CI 1.11 to 1.44).
source_locator: Results section, meta-analysis paragraph and Figure 2 (JAMIA 2012;19(1):121-127; PMC3240751).
short_exact_excerpt: The risk ratio was 1.26 (95% CI 1.11 to 1.44); erroneous advice was more likely to be followed in the CDSS groups than in the control groups
limitations: Four studies; 'small, indicative'; pre-generative-AI decision support; tools not outside advisors.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: any authoritative input (including an outside advisor's report) can anchor recipients and propagate its errors. In diligence, an advisor's traceable but wrong assumption could be adopted more readily if presented authoritatively. Needs testing with advisor reports rather than CDSS.
analyst_inference: Supports the need to measure error-propagation (adopting advisor errors) separately from overall accuracy.

proposition_tested: P1.6 (accountability) and expertise moderation: accountability and experience modulate over-reliance on decision support.
observed_finding: Mediators of automation bias included task-specific and DSS experience (8 papers), trust (increases reliance) and confidence (decreases reliance), workload, task complexity, and time pressure. Task inexperience may lead to automation-related errors, yet inexperienced users showed the greatest overall improvement from DSS. Accountability: two studies found external manipulation of accountability increased vigilance and reduced automation bias; another found external manipulation had no effect but users' internal perception of accountability did.
population_and_setting: 74 studies; healthcare, aviation, generic tasks; mixed expertise.
study_or_observation_method: Narrative synthesis/vote counting.
outcome_measured: Automation bias errors by mediator.
quantitative_result: Counts of studies only (e.g., experience in 8 papers; accountability: 2 studies positive for external manipulation, 1 null for external but positive for perceived accountability).
source_locator: Discussion sections 'Experience', 'Confidence and trust', 'Task type', 'Implementation factors' (PMC3240751).
short_exact_excerpt: people who perceived themselves to be accountable made less AB errors
limitations: Accountability evidence comes from a handful of mostly aviation/laboratory studies (refs 45, 46, 65; e.g., Skitka, Mosier & Burdick 2000), not verified at primary-source level here.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Accountable professionals (credit officers, IC members personally answerable for approvals) may verify more than lab participants, so lab overreliance rates likely overstate risk in the target setting - but time pressure and workload (deal cadence) push the other way. Both moderators must be measured in any target-domain study.
analyst_inference: Suggests accountability is a lever that sustains review; a product that diffuses felt accountability (e.g., 'the system checked it') could increase automation bias. Hypothesis.

proposition_tested: P-NEW (measurement): Decision switching from correct to incorrect after advice ('negative consultation') is the cleanest measure of over-reliance.
observed_finding: The review identifies outcome measures used: negative consultations (correct pre-advice decision changed to incorrect post-advice), percentage of erroneous advice followed, accuracy drops when DSS is inaccurate, and DSS-user accuracy correlation; it states negative consultations are the clearest measure because other measures can be conflated by users sharing the same incorrect pre-advice decision.
population_and_setting: As WS7-E18.
study_or_observation_method: Methods synthesis.
outcome_measured: Measurement approaches.
source_locator: Results, 'Non-controlled effects - negative consultations' paragraph (PMC3240751).
short_exact_excerpt: Negative consultations are the clearest measure of AB
transferability_to_target_workflow: Requires capturing the reviewer's pre-advice judgment - feasible in diligence experiments (e.g., reviewer estimates key metric or flags issues before seeing advisor report).
analyst_inference: Same logic as Schemmer's sequential design (WS7-E17).

proposition_tested: P2.1/P2.2 Evidence presented in an easy-to-verify form reduces over-reliance (verification-cost mechanism).
observed_finding: In a maze task with a simulated AI, explanations rendered as path highlights on the maze (easy to check) produced lower overreliance than the same content rendered as written step-by-step text (hard to check), in both medium and hard mazes; written explanations did not reduce overreliance relative to prediction-only. Authors argue null results in the literature may arise because explanations do not sufficiently reduce the cost of verifying the AI's prediction.
population_and_setting: Prolific crowdworkers; total N=731 across 5 studies; Study 2 N=340 (170 highlight from Study 1, 170 written).
study_or_observation_method: Between-subjects; Bayesian regression models (specification in appendix).
intervention_and_comparator: Highlight explanation vs written explanation (Study 2); explanation vs prediction-only across task difficulty (Study 1).
outcome_measured: Overreliance (agreeing with AI when it is wrong); exploratory accuracy.
quantitative_result: Study 2, Highlight minus Written: medium maze mean -1.63 (95% CI -2.78 to -0.559); hard maze -1.632 (95% CI -2.570 to -0.694) (model-scale estimates; units per appendix model, not extracted).
source_locator: Abstract p. 1; Section 6 Study 2, Table 3 and Fig. 9, p. 18; Fig. 8 caption p. 16.
short_exact_excerpt: Our results suggest that some of the null effects found in literature could be due in part to the explanation not sufficiently reducing the costs of verifying the AI’s prediction.
limitations: Artificial task with unambiguous, visually checkable ground truth; lay participants; units of effect on model scale.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Strongest mechanism-level support found for P2.1/P2.2: what matters is whether the presentation makes checking cheaper than re-deriving. Diligence analogue: a pinpoint link from an advisor's claim to the exact contract clause/data series (cheap check) vs a narrative justification (costly check). Must be tested in realistic documents where checking a source still requires judgment.
analyst_inference: Highlights here are closer to 'showing the evidence path' (X2/X3) than to persuasive rationale (X1); this is the most relevant experimental analogue to traceability, but still not source citation in the legal/financial sense.

proposition_tested: P2.1 qualified: explanation benefit appears only when the task is effortful enough that checking the explanation saves effort.
observed_finding: Study 1 found explanations did not produce an observable reduction in overreliance in easy or medium mazes but did reduce overreliance in the hard maze; exploratory analysis found explanations increased accuracy in the hard task. Monetary incentives (Study 4) also affected overreliance.
population_and_setting: Prolific crowdworkers; Study 1 N=340.
study_or_observation_method: Between-subjects, Bayesian models.
intervention_and_comparator: Explanation vs prediction-only, crossed with maze difficulty.
outcome_measured: Overreliance; accuracy (exploratory).
quantitative_result: Not extracted numerically for Study 1 in this timebox.
source_locator: Section 5 Study 1 results/summary, p. 16.
short_exact_excerpt: In summary, explanations do not produce an observable reduction in overreliance in easy or medium tasks, but do reduce overreliance in the hard task.
limitations: As WS7-E21.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Diligence reviews are effortful (large reports, models), the condition under which verification aids helped here; but stakes and incentives also differ.

proposition_tested: P2.1/P2.2 qualified; P2.3: explanations help only insofar as they enable verification, which many tasks do not permit.
observed_finding: Theory paper synthesizing prior experiments: explanations are useful only to the extent they allow the decision maker to verify the correctness of the AI's prediction; prior studies find explanations often do not facilitate verification; most tasks fundamentally do not allow easy verification regardless of explanation method. Distinguishes outcome-graded from strategy-graded reliance.
population_and_setting: Literature on AI-advised decision making.
study_or_observation_method: Theoretical argument with review of prior studies.
source_locator: Abstract, p. 1 (arXiv v4).
short_exact_excerpt: we argue explanations are only useful to the extent that they allow a human decision maker to verify the correctness of the AI’s prediction.
limitations: Only abstract/introduction reviewed; theory, not new data.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Frames the key question for the thesis: which diligence claims are verifiable by source lookup (contract terms, permits, interconnection agreements, historical data) vs inherently judgmental (degradation, merchant price forecasts, curtailment). Traceability can only lower cost for the former.
analyst_inference: Predicts that traceability benefits will be concentrated in W2 for verifiable factual claims and small for forecast/judgment claims (W1).

proposition_tested: P-NEW: Expertise reduces but does not eliminate adoption of incorrect advice.
observed_finding: In a prospective reader experiment, 27 radiologists assigned BI-RADS categories to mammograms with suggestions purportedly from AI; 12 of 40 test cases carried incorrect suggestions. Inexperienced radiologists were correct in almost 80% of cases with correct suggestions but under 20% with incorrect ones; experienced radiologists (more than 15 years on average) fell from 82% to 45.5%. The lead author recommended ensuring users feel accountable for their decisions as a mitigation.
population_and_setting: 27 radiologists of varying experience (Germany/Netherlands), mammography BI-RADS assessment.
study_or_observation_method: Prospective experiment; training set of 10 correct suggestions then 40 cases with 12 incorrect suggestions.
intervention_and_comparator: Correct vs incorrect purported-AI BI-RADS suggestions, by reader experience.
outcome_measured: Accuracy of BI-RADS assignment.
quantitative_result: Inexperienced: ~80% correct with correct suggestion vs <20% with incorrect suggestion. Experienced (>15 yrs avg): 82% vs 45.5%. Moderately experienced group and statistics not reported in press release.
source_locator: RSNA press release, 2023-05-02, paragraphs 3-5.
short_exact_excerpt: Experienced radiologists—those with more than 15 years of experience on average—saw their accuracy fall from 82% to 45.5% when the purported AI suggested the incorrect category.
limitations: Press release only; simulated AI; error rate (30% of cases) far higher than typical deployments; no unaided-reader comparator for the same cases reported in release.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Professional participants, high-stakes perceptual judgment. Transfers as: even senior reviewers anchor on authoritative input. In diligence, senior credit staff reviewing an advisor's conclusions may still adopt embedded errors; experience is partial protection.
analyst_inference: Counters the assumption that lay-sample overreliance disappears with expert recipients.

proposition_tested: P2.3 (measurement): subjective trust/preference and proxy tasks do not predict actual decision performance.
observed_finding: Two online experiments and one think-aloud study found that evaluations of explainable AI using proxy tasks (e.g., predicting the AI's decision from its explanation) did not predict results with actual decision-making tasks, and subjective trust/preference measures did not predict objective performance on the same tasks.
population_and_setting: Online lay participants and in-person think-aloud participants (details not extracted).
study_or_observation_method: Comparison of evaluation methods.
intervention_and_comparator: Proxy-task evaluation vs actual-task evaluation; subjective vs objective measures.
outcome_measured: Concordance of evaluation methods.
quantitative_result: Not extracted (abstract only reviewed).
source_locator: Abstract, p. 1.
short_exact_excerpt: the subjective measures on evaluations with actual decision-making tasks did not predict the objective performance on those same tasks.
limitations: Abstract-level review only.
transferability_to_target_workflow: User surveys of diligence professionals ('the traceable report saved me time / I trust it more') cannot substitute for objective error-detection measurement.
analyst_inference: Combined with WS7-E13, a strong methodological caution against using stated preference as evidence for RQ2.

proposition_tested: P-NEW: Professional recipients' reliance on contradictory expert evidence depends on the perceived source (AI vs human specialist), not only on content - a source cue can produce under-reliance.
observed_finding: In an experiment, auditors who received contradictory evidence about management's complex estimate from their firm's AI system, rather than from a human specialist (otherwise identical advice), proposed smaller adjustments to management's estimates, particularly when management's estimate used relatively objective inputs. Authors interpret this as algorithm aversion that could be costly.
evidence_type: controlled experiment with auditor participants (abstract only)
population_and_setting: Auditors (number and rank not reviewed) evaluating a complex accounting estimate.
study_or_observation_method: Experiment manipulating evidence source (AI system vs human specialist) and objectivity of management's inputs.
intervention_and_comparator: Contradictory evidence attributed to firm's AI system vs to a human specialist; objective vs subjective management inputs.
outcome_measured: Proposed audit adjustment to management's estimate.
quantitative_result: Not available from abstract.
source_locator: Abstract (UNLV Digital Scholarship repository page).
short_exact_excerpt: auditors receiving contradictory evidence from their firm's AI system (instead of a human specialist) propose smaller adjustments to management's complex estimates
limitations: Abstract only; no ground truth for 'correct' adjustment stated in abstract; hypothetical case.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Professional participants in an advisor-like structure (specialist evidence -> auditor -> opinion). Transfers as: recipients weight outside evidence by perceived source legitimacy; an AI-produced or tool-produced diligence output may be discounted relative to a named human expert even if identical, so traceability products may need human attribution/accountability to be relied upon. Opposite failure mode to automation bias.
analyst_inference: Important counterweight to lab overreliance findings (WS7-E08, E12): in professional settings, under-reliance on machine-produced evidence is also documented, so 'reduced review' cannot be assumed from better evidence; source identity and accountability matter.

proposition_tested: P2.4 (coverage/structure visibility improves recipient use) and P2.3 (format raises acceptance without decision benefit)
observed_finding: Referring clinicians and radiologists rated structured body-CT reports higher than conventional reports for content and clarity; ratings of the report's effectiveness in advancing the patient's position on the clinical spectrum (POCS grade) did not differ significantly.
evidence_type: direct evidence (medical analogy); stated preference/ratings, not observed behavior
population_and_setting: 11 physicians (3 radiologists, 3 fellows, 3 surgeons, 2 medical oncologists) at a US tertiary cancer center; 330 body CT reports
study_or_observation_method: Quality-improvement comparison; each rater read 15 conventional and 15 structured reports; mixed-effects models
intervention_and_comparator: Structured (template) reports (Jun-Sep 2009) vs conventional free-form reports (Jan-Jun 2009), different patients
outcome_measured: Satisfaction with content and clarity (1-10); POCS grade (I-IV coded 1-5)
source_locator: Abstract (Results, Conclusion); Results sections 'Satisfaction with Content', 'Satisfaction with Clarity', 'Radiology Report Grading Scale'
short_exact_excerpt: Referring clinicians and radiologists found that structured reports had better content and greater clarity than conventional reports.
limitations: Ratings, not correctness or downstream decision quality; no measure of clarification calls, reading time or errors; producer time not measured; single center.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a fixed, element-by-element diligence report layout may be rated clearer by IC members/lenders. Difference: satisfaction gains may not translate into better investment decisions (analogous to unchanged POCS grade). Verify: whether structured diligence reports change reviewer time, follow-up questions, or detection of issues, not just ratings.
analyst_inference: Clean example of satisfaction/clarity gain without a measured decision-utility gain; supports separating perceived usefulness from appropriate reliance.

proposition_tested: P4.1/P5.1 (templates require recipient-specific design input; standardization has setup cost)
observed_finding: Templates were built by a departmental committee with input from 16 multidisciplinary disease-management teams, covering 205 common examinations (43 CT protocols); authors consulted referring physicians and many attending radiologists and credit this involvement for user acceptance.
population_and_setting: Memorial Sloan-Kettering radiology department
study_or_observation_method: Description of template development in Methods/Discussion
outcome_measured: Number of templates; development process
quantitative_result: 205 templates; 43 CT protocols; 16 disease-management teams consulted
source_locator: Materials and Methods ('Structured Reporting Method'); Discussion
short_exact_excerpt: consulted with referring physicians to address their needs and concerns
limitations: Process description; cost/effort of development not quantified.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a coverage-map template for renewable diligence would need input from recipients (IC, lenders, tax equity) per asset class/stage, implying non-trivial setup and per-client variation. Verify: how many template variants a diligence provider needs across solar/wind/storage and client types.
analyst_inference: Suggests 'standardized' templates are locally co-designed with recipients; repeatability comes after a substantial design investment.

proposition_tested: P2.4 (structured/explicit-coverage reporting improves report use) - strength of evidence
observed_finding: A PRISMA-based review of 63 structured-reporting studies in radiology found most report improvement, but only one study (two papers, Johnson 2009/2010) reached the highest evidence level and that study found no improvement; the remaining 61 were level B; heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis. Error outcomes were mixed (e.g., prepopulated templates did not affect error rate; checklist reduced some misses).
evidence_type: systematic review (narrative synthesis) of observational and interventional studies
population_and_setting: Radiology structured-reporting literature to Aug 2020 (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane)
study_or_observation_method: Systematic search, evidence grading (Siwek A/B/C), thematic synthesis
intervention_and_comparator: Structured reporting (layout: templates/checklists; content: point-and-click/decision trees) vs free text
outcome_measured: Varied: completeness, accuracy, satisfaction, reporting time, billing
quantitative_result: 8,561 screened; 63 studies included; 2 papers (1 study) level A; 61 level B. No pooled effect estimate.
source_locator: Abstract; Results; 'Level of evidence' section; Table 1
short_exact_excerpt: The level of evidence for implementing SR in radiology is still low and outcomes should be interpreted with caution.
limitations: Narrative synthesis; outcome categories not tallied; publication bias likely.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism transferring: structure is widely believed to help, but rigorous evidence is thin even in a field with decades of study. Verify in diligence: controlled comparisons (same deals, structured vs narrative reports) rather than adoption anecdotes.
analyst_inference: The best-designed study in the field is negative; the positive literature is mostly before/after or rating studies. This is a meaningful caution for P2.4.

proposition_tested: P5.1 (standardized formats improve repeatability) and P-NEW: structured format effects are confounded with content standardization
observed_finding: The reviewers note that many studies built templates through expert meetings or literature review (confounding format with content standardization) and question whether structured reporting improves reporting or is 'only a means in facilitating standardization'; reporting-time results were mixed (some shorter, some no effect).
population_and_setting: Radiology SR literature
study_or_observation_method: Thematic synthesis
outcome_measured: Reporting time; standardization
quantitative_result: No pooled estimate; individual studies mixed on dictation/reporting time.
source_locator: Discussion; Conclusion; Table 1 entries (Hawkins 2012; Hanna 2016; Kim 2020)
short_exact_excerpt: questionable whether SR is the solution for improving reporting in radiology or only a means in facilitating standardization
limitations: Authors' interpretation; no causal decomposition.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: in diligence, gains attributed to a 'coverage map' format may really come from agreeing on what must be checked (scope standard). Verify: separate effects of an agreed checklist of diligence items from the presentation format.
analyst_inference: Important for the thesis: the active ingredient may be the agreed list of required elements (scope definition), not the visible structure per se.

proposition_tested: P2.4 / P2.2 (structured reporting improves completeness/accuracy) - counterevidence; cost of structure
observed_finding: Residents who switched to a structured reporting system (SRS) produced less accurate and less complete reports on re-reading the same cases, while control residents using free-text dictation improved; residents complained the SRS was overly constraining and time-consuming.
evidence_type: direct evidence (medical analogy); controlled cohort with criterion-standard grading
population_and_setting: Radiology residents (16 control, 18 intervention); 25 brain MR cases (suspected stroke)
study_or_observation_method: Two-phase cohort; phase 2 four months later; neuroradiologist grading against consensus and >=6-month follow-up criterion standard
intervention_and_comparator: Point-and-click structured reporting system vs conventional free-text dictation
outcome_measured: Report accuracy and completeness scores; resident opinions
quantitative_result: Intervention group: accuracy 91.5 -> 88.7, completeness 68.7 -> 54.3; control group: accuracy 91.4 -> 92.4, completeness 67.8 -> 71.7 (all P<.001).
source_locator: Abstract (Results, Conclusion)
short_exact_excerpt: such changes cannot be assumed to improve report accuracy or completeness. Any SRS should be tested for effect on intrinsic report quality.
limitations: Abstract only; early SRS software; residents; small n; nonrandomized allocation.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a rigid structured diligence template can crowd out salient narrative findings and cost producer time. Verify: whether rigid checklists in technical/IE diligence reduce reporting of non-template issues (e.g., site-specific geotech or interconnection quirks).
analyst_inference: Strongest direct counterevidence in this workstream: structure that constrains the producer can lower completeness of what matters.

proposition_tested: P2.4 (explicit element lists improve report completeness, X5) - completeness vs clinical impact
observed_finding: Across 33 observational studies, synoptic pathology reporting was associated with higher overall completeness in 13 of 14 studies measuring it; gains concentrated in elements narrative reports often omitted (e.g., resection margins, lymphovascular/perineural invasion), whereas core elements like tumour type and nodal status were already adequately reported in narrative reports. Clinical impact had not been demonstrated.
population_and_setting: Cancer pathology reports (10 tumour types; mostly colorectal n=16, breast n=9)
study_or_observation_method: Systematic review (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane to 2015-09-30), 2 reviewers
intervention_and_comparator: Synoptic (checklist/template) reports vs narrative reports
outcome_measured: Completeness of required parameters (>90% = sufficient)
quantitative_result: Overall completeness up in 13/14 studies (exception: Hassell et al.). Example (Beattie, colorectal): resection margins 54% -> 100%; vascular invasion 68% -> 100%; perineural invasion 52% -> 98%; stage 39% -> 100%; nodal status 85% -> 99%.
source_locator: Results ('Overall completeness', 'Parameter-specific completeness'); Fig. 2; Table 3; Abstract
short_exact_excerpt: Demonstration of clinical impact of this improved method of pathology reporting is required
limitations: Observational designs; publication bias possible; completeness is a report property, not recipient decision quality.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: an explicit required-element list most helps for items producers otherwise skip (in diligence: e.g., stating that a title exception, curtailment risk or warranty gap was checked). Verify: which diligence items are routinely omitted in narrative reports; whether listing them changes lender/IC decisions.
analyst_inference: Completeness (X5 of report) improves reliably; recipient benefit is inferred, not measured. Gains are item-specific, implying a targeted list may capture most value.

proposition_tested: P5.1 (standardization) - producer burden and inflexibility
observed_finding: The review reports adoption barriers: pathologist preference for narrative flexibility, workflow disruption, EHR integration problems, and delays from changing criteria/interfaces; one included study found pathologists found synoptic reporting more difficult and inflexible with some parameters missed, and was the only study where synoptic reports were less complete.
population_and_setting: Pathology departments in included studies
study_or_observation_method: Narrative discussion
outcome_measured: Adoption barriers; completeness
quantitative_result: One study (Hassell et al.) with lower completeness under SR; progesterone receptor completeness decreased in another (McEvoy).
source_locator: Discussion paragraph 4; Results ('Parameter-specific completeness'); Fig. 2
limitations: Qualitative; no time/cost measures.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: template rigidity and IT integration are recurring costs; in diligence, templates must integrate with data rooms/report tools. Verify: producer time and integration cost per deliverable.
analyst_inference: Costs fall mainly on producers (and IT), not recipients.

proposition_tested: P2.4/P5.1 (checklists listing required elements associate with complete reports)
observed_finding: In 86 institutions, 68.8% of cancer reports contained all elements required by the ACS Commission on Cancer; institutions routinely using checklists had complete reports far more often (88%) than those not using them (34%); institutions with error-tracking systems also did better (88% vs 68%). Extent of invasion and margin status were the most commonly missing elements.
population_and_setting: 2125 breast, colon, rectum, prostate cancer reports from 86 Q-Probes institutions
study_or_observation_method: Each institution reviewed 25 consecutive reports for missing required elements
intervention_and_comparator: Routine checklist use vs no routine checklist use (institution-level)
outcome_measured: Proportion of reports with all required elements
quantitative_result: 68.8% of 2125 reports complete; checklist institutions 88% vs non-checklist 34%; error-tracking 88% vs 68%.
source_locator: Abstract (Results, Conclusions)
short_exact_excerpt: Institutions in which checklists were routinely used reported all required elements at a higher rate than those that did not use checklists (88% versus 34%)
limitations: Correlational; institution-level confounding (quality culture); self-audit.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: diligence providers that use an explicit required-item checklist may omit fewer required items. Verify: omission rates in actual diligence deliverables with vs without checklists; whether recipients' own checklists (lender requirements) already serve this role.
analyst_inference: About 30% of narrative-era reports missed required elements - suggests recipients (oncologists) would otherwise need to chase missing items (W3), but the study does not measure follow-up queries.

proposition_tested: P2.4 (complete, structured reports improve recipient ability to use them)
observed_finding: Structured pancreatic CT reports contained more of 12 key staging/surgical-planning features; two of three surgeons found planning information easily accessible far more often with structured reports (third: no significant difference), all three judged information sufficient for surgical planning more often, and surgeons were more likely to convert 'unsure' resectability judgments into definitive answers.
evidence_type: retrospective before/after with blinded recipient (surgeon) evaluation
population_and_setting: Presurgical multiphasic pancreatic CT reports at one US institution; 48 structured, 72 nonstructured; 3 pancreatic surgeons
study_or_observation_method: Report content audit for 12 features; surgeons rated reports alone and with images
intervention_and_comparator: Disease-specific structured template (from Apr 2008) vs nonstructured reports
outcome_measured: Key features present; ease of extracting; sufficiency for planning; resectability certainty
quantitative_result: Features: 10.6 +/- 0.9 (structured) vs 7.3 +/- 2.1 (nonstructured), P<.001. Easily accessible: 94%/60%/98% vs 47%/54%/32% (P<.001, .79, <.001). Sufficient for planning: 96%/69%/98% vs 31%/43%/25% (P<.001, .009, <.001).
source_locator: Abstract (Results)
short_exact_excerpt: Surgeons had sufficient information for surgical planning in 96%, 69%, and 98% of structured and 31%, 43%, and 25% of nonstructured reports
limitations: Abstract only; sufficiency is surgeon judgment; no measured decision accuracy, clarification calls, or patient outcomes; inter-surgeon variation large.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism closest to the target: a recipient-specific template listing every decision-relevant element reduces gaps the decision-maker must fill (e.g., IC needing interconnection status, offtake terms, resource P50/P90). Verify: whether IC members/lenders report fewer information requests and more definitive go/no-go judgments with element-complete diligence reports.
analyst_inference: Best direct evidence that recipient-defined element lists improve recipient usability; 'more definitive' is not 'more correct'.

proposition_tested: P2.2 (structured checklists improve detection of omissions) - producer-side
observed_finding: A mandatory checklist-style template for resident cervical-spine CT reports was associated with fewer misses of non-fracture emergent findings (and lung findings) but not of fractures; the overall reduction was not statistically significant.
population_and_setting: Resident preliminary C-spine CT reports at a level-one trauma center; 2,913 reports
study_or_observation_method: Pre/post comparison; misses confirmed by attending neuroradiologist
intervention_and_comparator: Mandatory checklist template vs prior free-form preliminary reports
outcome_measured: Missed emergent findings
source_locator: Results; Table 1; Abstract
short_exact_excerpt: Our findings suggest that the use of checklists in structured reporting may increase diagnostic accuracy.
limitations: Single program; cohort changes; Hawthorne effect; underpowered.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: forcing producers to address each listed item (incl. 'no issue') reduces misses of peripheral items outside the main question (in diligence: secondary risks outside the headline scope). It did not help the primary search task (fractures). Verify: whether checklist-based diligence reduces missed secondary issues without degrading primary analysis.
analyst_inference: Coverage checklists act on producer attention to 'satisfaction of search' items - benefit is to the recipient only indirectly via fewer omissions.

proposition_tested: P2.4 qualified / P2.5 analog: prefilled 'normal'/'checked-no finding' text does not guarantee correctness
observed_finding: Prepopulated standard (normal) report templates did not change error rate or dictation time compared with a week without them; among errors, 39 of 2,012 (1.9%) were retained template statements contradicting dictated findings or impression.
population_and_setting: Pediatric radiology department (Cincinnati Children's); 12,387 reports, 1,173 randomly sampled
study_or_observation_method: Week 1 prepopulated templates enabled vs week 2 disabled; 11 error types coded
intervention_and_comparator: Prepopulated templates vs no prepopulation
outcome_measured: Errors per report; dictation time
quantitative_result: Errors/report 1.70 vs 1.73; reports with nongrammatical error 33% vs 36% (p=0.71 for nongrammatical rate); median dictation time 4 min (IQR 2-10) both weeks (p=0.92). Template-contradiction commission errors: 39 (1.9% of 2,012 errors; 0.03/report), pooled across weeks.
source_locator: Abstract; Results; Table 1 (error types)
short_exact_excerpt: Retained statement from a standardized template that contradicts the dictated findings or impression
limitations: Two weeks only; pooled error categories; manual coding.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: default 'checked - no issue found' entries in a diligence coverage map can be left unedited and become false negatives. Verify: whether diligence templates have prefilled 'no exceptions' text and how often it contradicts body findings; require evidence links per 'no issue' entry.
analyst_inference: A pertinent-negative entry is only as good as the check behind it; template defaults create a specific new error mode.

proposition_tested: P2.4 (explicit pertinent negatives valued by recipients) - stated preference
observed_finding: When an abnormality was identified, pertinent negatives were deemed useful by 89% of clinicians and 92% of radiologists; both groups preferred moderate/detailed reports over limited ones, while itemized vs prose format made no significant difference.
population_and_setting: Clinicians (89/183, 49%) and radiologists (31/58, 53%) at London Health Sciences Centre, Ontario
study_or_observation_method: Mailed survey, three lumbar spine CT/MR scenarios x six report variants (content level x format)
intervention_and_comparator: Limited vs moderate vs detailed content; prose vs itemized
outcome_measured: Satisfaction (1-5); opinions on report components
quantitative_result: Pertinent negatives useful: clinicians 89%, radiologists 92% (when abnormality present). Case 1 clinician means ~2.1-2.2 (limited) vs 4.0-4.1 (detailed). Detail preferred over limited (P<.01). Format: no significant preference.
source_locator: Results > Report Content > Radiologists versus Clinicians; Conclusions
short_exact_excerpt: When an abnormality was identified, pertinent negatives were deemed useful by both clinicians (89%) and radiologists (92%).
limitations: Stated preference; hypothetical reports; single center.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: recipients say they value explicit 'checked and absent' statements next to positive findings. Verify in diligence: whether IC/lenders actually use 'no issue found' entries to skip re-checks (observed behavior), not just say they value them.
analyst_inference: Content completeness (incl. pertinent negatives) mattered more to recipients than layout - aligns with WS8-E04 confounding point.

proposition_tested: P5.1 (standardized formats make delivery repeatable) - with customization burden
observed_finding: A 36-radiologist pediatric department created 228 standardized structured reports over ~2 years, covering 94% of study volume; after implementation, audits showed 100% adherence to the standard format and 99% adherence to the normal report when studies were normal; each report was vetted by all radiologists who would use it.
population_and_setting: Tertiary children's hospital radiology department (36 radiologists), Feb 2010 - Sep 2011
study_or_observation_method: Work group, guidelines/checklists, subcommittee review, vetting by users, quarterly audits, survey
intervention_and_comparator: Department-wide standardized structured reporting vs prior practice
outcome_measured: Number of templates; volume coverage; adherence to format and normal report
quantitative_result: 228 templates; 199,000 of 212,000 studies (94%) by volume; 223/223 (100%) audited reports adhered to format; 80/81 (99%) adhered to normal report.
source_locator: Abstract (Results)
short_exact_excerpt: A total of 228 standardized structured reports were created within 2 years after initiation of the project, corresponding to 199,000 (94%) of 212,000 departmental studies by volume.
limitations: Abstract only; adherence measures format conformance, not accuracy or recipient benefit; enthusiastic single site.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: delivery can become highly repeatable once a template library exists, but building it required hundreds of templates and consensus vetting. Verify: number of template variants and time-to-library for a diligence provider; whether adherence translates into recipient time savings.
analyst_inference: Repeatability achievable, but via substantial one-time internal standardization labor; relevant to P5.1 supplier economics only by analogy.

proposition_tested: P5.1/P4.1 (standardization in practice remains adaptable/local)
observed_finding: Among 265 responding academic radiologists, 51.3% were in groups with structured reports for at least half of reports; only 13% used rigid unmodifiable structures or checklists rather than adaptable outlines; 59.5% were satisfied with their structured reports; respondents also reported strong opinions about limitations.
population_and_setting: Association of University Radiologists members (North America), 265/910 responded (29.1%)
study_or_observation_method: Online survey
outcome_measured: Prevalence and type of structured reporting; satisfaction
quantitative_result: 51.3% SR for >= half of reports; 10.9% none; 13% rigid/unmodifiable; 59.5% satisfied vs 13% dissatisfied.
source_locator: Abstract (Results)
short_exact_excerpt: A significantly fewer 13% of respondents used rigid unmodifiable structures or checklists rather than adaptable outlines
limitations: Abstract only; low response; academic skew.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: even where 'structured reporting' is common, producers keep adaptable outlines - standardization is partial. Verify: whether diligence providers' 'standard' reports are in fact adaptable outlines with heavy per-deal narrative.
analyst_inference: Supports view that delivery standardization plateaus at flexible outlines; rigid checklists are a minority.

proposition_tested: P5.1 (standard templates cover only part of real report content)
observed_finding: Five RSNA reporting templates accounted for only 17-49% of the concepts that actually appeared in corresponding free-text reports from one academic center.
population_and_setting: 8,275 consecutive de-identified radiology reports at one academic center; 5 RSNA templates
study_or_observation_method: RadLex/SNOMED CT annotation and concept overlap
intervention_and_comparator: Template concept set vs free-text report concepts
outcome_measured: Share of report concepts covered by templates
quantitative_result: 17% to 49% of concepts covered, depending on template.
source_locator: Abstract
short_exact_excerpt: The reporting templates we examined accounted for 17 to 49 % of the concepts that actually appeared in a sample of corresponding radiology reports.
limitations: Abstract only; concept frequency is not clinical importance; authors read result as useful coverage.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a published standard template covers a core but leaves much report content to local/free text - analogous to residual bespoke narrative in diligence. Verify: share of a diligence report that maps to a standard coverage list vs bespoke content.
analyst_inference: Implies significant residual customization even with a professional-society template library.

proposition_tested: P2.4/P5.1 (explicit element-response reporting incl. 'not applicable'; permitted local customization)
observed_finding: CAP accreditation requires all required data elements of applicable cancer protocols, with responses in synoptic element-response format, in at least 90% of definitive resection reports, with annual self-audit; core elements must be reported whether applicable or not and 'Cannot be determined' is an allowed response. Laboratories may alter wording and responses, list elements in any order, add items, and implement at institutional discretion; system use requires a license; new/revised protocols have an 8-month adoption window.
population_and_setting: CAP-accredited US laboratories
study_or_observation_method: Document review
outcome_measured: Required report content and permitted flexibility
quantitative_result: Threshold: >=90% of definitive resection reports; 8-month adoption window.
source_locator: FAQ items: 'What are the CAP accreditation program requirements...', 'What is a synoptic report?', 'Do I need to list the data elements and responses exactly...', 'When new or revised cancer protocols are released...'
short_exact_excerpt: All core elements must be reported whether applicable or not.
limitations: Shows obligation and allowed flexibility, not compliance or recipient effects.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a binding element list with mandatory explicit responses (including not applicable / cannot be determined) is the medical equivalent of a diligence coverage map with 'checked - not applicable/insufficient data' entries. Difference: CAP leverage comes from accreditation; diligence has no equivalent mandatory standard. Verify: whether lenders' or IE scopes impose element lists; who would enforce them.
analyst_inference: Standardization is enforced on content (elements) while format/wording remain locally customizable - a model for 'standard core + local wrapper'.

proposition_tested: P5.1 (standards do not guarantee uniform delivery)
observed_finding: In a random sample of 1,618 VA pathology reports (2019-2021) for four cancers, 48% used synoptic format: 77% of resections but 19% of biopsies (range 97% colorectal resections to 0.5% colon biopsies); several core elements remained underdocumented.
evidence_type: observational audit (random sample across a national system)
population_and_setting: US Department of Veterans Affairs pathology reports: melanoma, colon, bladder, kidney cancer
study_or_observation_method: Random sampling of >=200 biopsy and >=200 resection reports per cancer
outcome_measured: Synoptic format use; core element documentation
quantitative_result: 778/1618 (48%; 95% CI 46-50%) synoptic; resections 621/811 (77%; 74-79%); biopsies 157/807 (19%; 17-22%); colorectal resections 200/206 (97%); colon biopsies 1/200 (0.5%).
source_locator: Abstract (Results)
short_exact_excerpt: Synoptic reporting was used about three-quarters of the time for resections and about 1 in 5 times for biopsies.
limitations: Abstract only; one system; does not measure consequences.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: uptake of standard formats concentrates where an external requirement applies (resections) and lags elsewhere. Verify: in diligence, whether standard coverage formats appear only where lenders/rating agencies require them.
analyst_inference: Analyst inference: accreditation requirements (CAP/CoC) apply to definitive resections, which plausibly explains the resection/biopsy gap - the abstract does not test this.

proposition_tested: P1.1 (review persists via institutional policy) and P1.3 (rework from inaccurate outside output)
observed_finding: Johns Hopkins requires second-opinion review of outside surgical pathology before treating referred patients; over 21 months, 86 of 6,171 reviewed cases (1.4%) had a changed diagnosis causing major modification in therapy or prognosis, with higher rates for serosal surfaces (9.5%) and female reproductive tract (5.1%). The authors note the practice was threatened by managed-care cost containment and recommend review before major therapy.
evidence_type: prospective case series at a referral center
population_and_setting: Outside surgical pathology referred to Johns Hopkins Hospital, Apr 1995 - Dec 1996
study_or_observation_method: Prospective collection; changed diagnosis = discordance with major therapy/prognosis modification (grade/stage changes excluded)
intervention_and_comparator: Mandatory second review of outside slides (no comparator)
outcome_measured: Changed diagnoses
quantitative_result: 86/6171 (1.4%) changed diagnoses; serosal surfaces 9.5% (P<0.0001), female reproductive tract 5.1% (P<0.0001); breast 1.4%; GI 1.2%; lung 0.6%.
source_locator: Abstract (Background, Methods, Results, Conclusions)
short_exact_excerpt: Of 6171 cases reviewed, second opinion surgical pathology resulted in 86 changed diagnoses (1.4%).
limitations: Abstract only; narrow definition excludes grade/stage changes; single center; old data.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: recipients with treatment authority re-review the underlying evidence (slides), not just the report, as a blanket policy, because rare errors are costly. In diligence, lenders' independent engineers re-reviewing sponsor reports may be similar. Verify: discrepancy rates found by IE/lender re-reviews and whether review is policy-blanket or risk-targeted.
analyst_inference: Low yield (1.4%) with blanket policy, but high consequence; review is justified by error cost, not report format. Re-review uses original evidence (slides) - traceability to raw evidence is what makes re-review possible.

proposition_tested: P1.1 (policy-mandated review) and P1.3 (rework from inaccurate output)
observed_finding: University of Iowa requires second opinion of outside surgical pathology slides before definitive treatment; of 5,629 cases, 132 (2.3%) had major and 507 (9.0%) minor diagnostic disagreements; 68 (1.2% of all cases) led to changes in clinical management on follow-up.
evidence_type: retrospective case series with clinical/pathologic follow-up
population_and_setting: Second-opinion surgical pathology cases at University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics
study_or_observation_method: Classification by second-opinion pathologist; follow-up for clinical significance
intervention_and_comparator: Mandatory second review (local standard of practice), no comparator
outcome_measured: Major/minor disagreements; management changes
quantitative_result: Major 132/5629 (2.3%); minor 507 (9.0%); management changed 68 (1.2% of total). Most major disagreements: female reproductive tract (32), GI tract (27), skin (24).
source_locator: Abstract
short_exact_excerpt: Of the 132 major diagnostic disagreements, 68 (1.2% of total cases reviewed) prompted changes in the clinical management as a result of the second opinion interpretation.
limitations: Abstract only; second-opinion pathologist judged disagreements; no cost or time data.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: blanket re-review policy whose yield is ~1% management-changing discrepancies. In diligence, analogous to lender re-review of advisor reports; verify actual yield and whether risk-targeting could cut work without missing material issues.
analyst_inference: Second, independent site with similar ~1.2-1.4% material-change rate; supports P1.1 and shows rework yield is low per case but persistent.

proposition_tested: P1.3 (quality-driven rework) alongside P1.1 (routine policy re-read)
observed_finding: At a Canadian tertiary center where all outside head and neck imaging is routinely re-read by a neuroradiologist before tumor board, second-opinion reports differed in stage from original reports in 56.4% of cases (90.6% of these were up-staging) and would change surgeon management recommendations in 38.3%; in 30 surgical cases, second-opinion stage agreed with pathology far more often than the original report.
population_and_setting: 94 consecutive head and neck cancer patients with outside CT/MR (2010), Calgary
study_or_observation_method: Three reviewers coded T/N/stage from each report; surgeon management recommendation per report; pathology as standard in surgical subgroup
intervention_and_comparator: Subspecialist second-opinion report vs original outside report
outcome_measured: Stage discrepancy; management discrepancy; agreement with pathologic stage
quantitative_result: Stage discrepancy 53/94 (56.4%; 95% CI 46.3-65.9%); management discrepancy 36/94 (38.3%; 29.1-48.4%); surgical subgroup stage agreement 40.0% (original) vs 93.3% (second opinion), P<.001; management agreement 33.3% vs 60.0%, P=.069.
source_locator: Results; Tables 2, 4, 5; Conclusion
short_exact_excerpt: subspecialty radiologist interpretation of imaging studies has a positive impact on patient care.
limitations: Small; non-blinded; second readers had more clinical information; no gold standard for non-surgical cases; costs not measured.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: when original reports are written for a general purpose and lack decision-specific elements (staging), recipients re-do the work. Diligence analog: generic third-party reports (e.g., a sponsor-commissioned study) re-scoped by a lender's adviser. Verify: share of lender re-work attributable to missing decision-specific elements vs disagreement on judgment.
analyst_inference: Analyst inference: high discrepancy here likely mixes missing staging elements (the second read was purpose-built for staging) with expertise differences; the authors do not separate them or mention structured reporting.

proposition_tested: P1.2 (avoidable reconstruction from missing evidence) and P2.1 (access to original evidence reduces redo)
observed_finding: Before chemoembolization, patients whose outside CT/MR images were unavailable or available only on CD/film (not imported) had much higher repeat-imaging rates than those whose images were imported into the local PACS; imported-image patients' repeat rate was similar to patients imaged only locally.
evidence_type: retrospective observational cohort with adjusted odds ratios
population_and_setting: 267 patients with abdominal CT/MRI within 4 months before transarterial chemoembolization at one US academic center
study_or_observation_method: Comparison of four groups by outside-image availability; multivariable adjustment (age, sex, referring institution, lesion size/number)
intervention_and_comparator: Outside images imported to PACS vs not available vs available but not imported vs all-local imaging
outcome_measured: Repeat imaging rate
quantitative_result: Repeat imaging: not available 13/18 (72%); available not imported 14/27 (52%); imported 9/79 (11%); local only 18/143 (13%). Adjusted OR vs imported: 31 (not available), 9.0 (not imported), both p<0.001; imported vs local OR 0.71, p=0.51.
source_locator: Abstract (Results)
short_exact_excerpt: When outside images were not available, 72% (13/18) of patients underwent repeat imaging; when outside images were available but not imported, 52% (14/27); when outside images were imported to PACS, 11% (9/79)
limitations: Abstract only; observational; small groups; residual confounding.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism strongly relevant: recipients redo work when the underlying evidence is not accessible in their own system, even if a report exists; integration into the recipient's workflow (PACS) - not just availability (CD) - cut redo to baseline. Diligence analog: providing source files/models in the client's tools vs PDFs. Verify: whether lenders re-run energy yield or financial models less often when native files are delivered and loaded into their systems.
analyst_inference: Distinguishes access (CD) from integration (PACS import): availability alone left 52% redo - supports RQ3-style integration value and P1.2. Note: re-imaging can also reflect clinical need for updated images.

proposition_tested: P3.1 (integration into recipient's system reduces recipient work end-to-end)
observed_finding: Images that were physically available but not imported into the recipient institution's PACS were associated with a 52% repeat-imaging rate, versus 11% when imported.
population_and_setting: Same as WS8-E21 (267 patients, one center)
study_or_observation_method: Group comparison with adjustment
intervention_and_comparator: Imported to PACS vs available on CD/film but not imported
outcome_measured: Repeat imaging
source_locator: Abstract (Results)
limitations: Same as above; the decision to import may correlate with other workflow factors.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: delivering an advisor's evidence in a form that loads into the recipient's own decision system may matter as much as delivering it at all. Verify: in diligence, compare re-work when deliverables are integrated into the client's data room/model templates vs delivered as standalone files.
analyst_inference: One of the few observed-behavior (not stated-preference) items here bearing on integration value; analogy only.

proposition_tested: P2.4 (explicit disclosure of data gaps/omissions) - regulatory requirement in a non-medical diligence report
observed_finding: The federal All Appropriate Inquiries rule requires the environmental professional's written report to include an opinion on conditions indicative of releases and an identification of data gaps that affect that ability; persons conducting the inquiry should identify data gaps, the sources consulted to address them, and comment on their significance; sampling may be conducted to address data gaps.
population_and_setting: US property acquirers seeking CERCLA landowner liability protections; environmental professionals
study_or_observation_method: Document review of 40 CFR 312.10, 312.20(g), 312.21(c)
outcome_measured: Required report content
source_locator: 40 CFR 312.10 (definition 'Data gap'); 312.20(g); 312.21(c)(1)-(2) (7-1-20 edition, GovInfo PDF)
short_exact_excerpt: should identify such data gaps, identify the sources of information consulted to address such data gaps, and comment upon the significance of such data gaps
limitations: Shows a disclosure obligation only; no evidence on how users act on data-gap disclosures. ASTM E1527-21 text not accessed.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a legally recognized diligence report with mandatory 'what we could not check and why it matters' disclosure exists in property transactions and is commonly part of renewable-project site diligence (Phase I ESAs). Verify: whether lenders/IC members actually read and act on data-gap sections, and whether similar disclosure is used in technical/IE reports.
analyst_inference: Closest non-medical precedent for coverage/omission visibility (X4) being codified; relevant as design precedent, not effect evidence.

proposition_tested: P1.1 (recipient retains independent obligations regardless of advisor report quality)
observed_finding: Under the AAI rule, the user (the acquiring party) must itself conduct certain inquiries - environmental cleanup liens (if not otherwise obtained), its own specialized knowledge or experience, the relationship of purchase price to fair market value, and commonly known or reasonably ascertainable information - and may provide that information to the environmental professional.
population_and_setting: Same as above
study_or_observation_method: Document review of 40 CFR 312.22
outcome_measured: Allocation of inquiry duties between user and professional
short_exact_excerpt: Persons identified under § 312.1(b) must conduct the inquiries listed in paragraphs (a)(1) through (a)(4) below
limitations: Obligation, not observed practice.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: some diligence work is structurally assigned to the recipient (user-specific knowledge, price relationship), so it persists however good the advisor's report is. Verify: equivalent recipient-retained duties in renewable lending (e.g., credit policy checks, KYC, sponsor knowledge).
analyst_inference: Formal allocation of retained work (W1/W4) that an advisor product cannot remove; supports P1.1.

proposition_tested: P5.1 (standardized lexicon/format makes outputs repeatable) - counterevidence on judgment variability
observed_finding: With the standardized BI-RADS lexicon and assessment categories, five breast radiologists showed only fair agreement on final assessment category (kappa 0.28) and slight agreement on mammographic mass density (kappa 0.18), though some ultrasound descriptors had substantial agreement (kappa 0.61-0.69).
population_and_setting: 94 biopsied breast lesions in 91 women; 5 radiologists; one US center
study_or_observation_method: Independent re-description and categorization; Cohen kappa; PPV against pathology
intervention_and_comparator: Standardized BI-RADS terminology (no comparator)
outcome_measured: Interobserver agreement; PPV of categories
quantitative_result: Final assessment kappa 0.28; mass density 0.18; calcification description 0.32; mass shape/margin 0.48; US orientation/shape/boundary 0.61/0.66/0.69. PPV: 4a 6/102 (6%), 4b 17/110 (15%), 4c 48/91 (53%), 5 71/78 (91%).
source_locator: Abstract (Results)
short_exact_excerpt: Fair agreement was obtained for final assessment category (kappa = 0.28).
limitations: Abstract only; enriched biopsy sample; older BI-RADS edition; authors characterize agreement as 'good'.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: standardizing the vocabulary and categories of a report does not standardize the judgment behind them; in diligence, a standard risk-rating scale may still yield inconsistent ratings across analysts. Verify: inter-analyst agreement on diligence risk ratings under a common template.
analyst_inference: Format repeatability (P5.1) is distinct from judgment repeatability; standard categories do make disagreement visible and comparable.

proposition_tested: P5.1 (standard templates adapted locally) and P2.2 (structured checklist reduces producer-side rework/omissions)
observed_finding: A head and neck CTA template built from RSNA informatics (RadReport) templates plus locally chosen critical findings to assess on all CTAs was associated with fewer attending revisions of residents' after-hours reports; authors attribute the reduction largely to typographical errors.
population_and_setting: Resident after-hours head and neck CTA reports at one academic center
study_or_observation_method: Baseline revision rate vs 2-month template availability period
intervention_and_comparator: Structured template (RSNA-based + local critical-findings list) vs unstructured dictation
outcome_measured: Proportion of resident reports revised by attending
quantitative_result: 10/41 (24%) unstructured vs 2/17 (12%) structured reports revised (~50% relative reduction); no p-value or CI reported in abstract.
source_locator: Abstract (Methods, Results, Conclusions)
short_exact_excerpt: The structured template was found to reduce revision rates by approximately 50% with 10/41 unstructured reports revised and 2/17 structured reports revised.
limitations: Tiny sample; no significance testing reported; revisions mostly immaterial (typographical); producer-side rework, not recipient clarification.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a published standard template is adopted only after local adaptation (adding institution-specific must-check items). Diligence analog: a standard coverage list plus client/asset-specific must-check items. Verify: proportion of template content that is local vs standard in diligence deliverables.
analyst_inference: Illustrates the 'standard core + local additions' customization pattern for RadReport; the rework effect is weak evidence. No direct study of recipient clarification calls was found (see search_log).

proposition_tested: P1.1 Retained review driven by formal obligations; also P1.2 (missing evidence from vendor)
observed_finding: Revised interagency MRM guidance states that vendor/third-party products (data, parameter values, complete models) remain subject to model risk management principles even though banks may not receive the vendor's code, data or methodology; sound practice includes validating vendor products (internally or by outside parties) and understanding conceptual soundness, design, development data and performance.
evidence_type: regulatory obligation (direct evidence of a formal requirement; not of compliance, cost, or effect)
population_and_setting: US banking organizations supervised by FRB, FDIC, OCC; models including vendor products
study_or_observation_method: Primary supervisory guidance text review
outcome_measured: Supervisory expectation for treatment of vendor models
source_locator: SR 26-2 Attachment, Section VII 'Vendor and Other Third-Party Products', printed pp. 11-12
short_exact_excerpt: because certain components may be proprietary, banking organizations may not receive from the vendor the underlying code, data, or methodology that they would have if a model were developed internally. Nevertheless, the principles of model risk management remain applicable.
limitations: Guidance, not a rule; scope is models, not advisory reports; tailoring to risk/size is explicitly permitted.
